In various situations, decisions made by artificial intelligence systems are difficult to interpret due to the lack of transparent explanations. Techniques like adversarial examples and explanation models attempt to address this issue, but successful models in practice often rely on simplified representations of the original complex classifier. Our study seeks to improve the understanding of decision-making processes within complex neural networks by identifying key attributes used to make predictions. A novel algorithm, feature effect algorithm, is introduced to pinpoint important attributes by training simple, symbolic models to replicate the behavior of black-box classifiers. These models, implemented using logic and decision trees, can provide insights into the decision-making processes of complex networks, as well as robustness against corruption or alteration of attribute values. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to data from two real-world datasets.

Over-smoothing is a well-documented issue in Graph Convolutional Networks, where repeated applications of the graph convolution operation lead to diminished feature maps. While this phenomenon has been studied in shallow networks, its effects on deeper networks, such as Graph Convolutional Networks with Residual Connections (GCRNs), are not yet fully understood. In this letter, we delve into the feature propagation dynamics of GCRNs and develop a mathematical framework to explain how the network's depth influences the dimensionality of the resulting feature maps. Our analysis, which is validated through experiments, provides valuable insights into the over-smoothing problem and can be employed to create high-performance, extremely deep GCRNs.

Dark matter may have been created during the heat death of the universe through a thermal equilibrium established by a mediator particle. To gain insight into such production processes, we develop simplified models of dark matter and mediator interactions and use machine learning to classify and explore the various possibilities. By applying these models, we identify the constraints on model types and parameter ranges in which dark matter can be effectively created through the heat death of the universe.

We introduce two new functions, one describing a probability distribution within a transverse plane and another a corresponding momentum distribution, both relative to the momentum of a parent hadron. These functions are linked to existing QCD factors and can be studied using exclusive processes involving a high-energy photon and a hadron, such as Zhadron scattering. This theoretical work marks the beginning of a new field of study.

This study demonstrates that specific spaces, including those derived from the Closed Long Ray and Long Line, possess the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property when paired with a vast array of spaces, including many based on Coxeter groups and their associated Euclidean spaces. Conversely, we will also show that a particular space, the Oriented Prismatic Curve, does not exhibit this property when paired with all spaces based on Coxeter groups, ultimately leading to a conclusion about its relationship with the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Invariant of the Euclidean space of n dimensions.

The unique properties of graphene make it an ideal substrate for growing a variety of epitaxial materials, with the epitaxial relationship between the material and graphene determined by the underlying atomic structure of a single layer of graphene. In this study, researchers investigated how changing the conditions under which graphene was grown - specifically by varying the temperature at which it was grown - affected the structure of epitaxial PbSe quantum dots, finding that changing the substrate conditions resulted in the formation of different epitaxial domains. Utilizing a range of investigative tools and techniques, such as 3D structural analysis and other state-of-the-art technologies, the researchers were able to provide an in-depth analysis of the structure of the epitaxial material and its relationship with the graphene substrate, revealing that altering the graphene substrate results in a corresponding transformation in the structural arrangement of the epitaxial material. Furthermore, the researchers found that changing the graphene substrate conditions resulted in the formation of epitaxial lead selenide microstructures with different properties and performance capabilities. By understanding how the graphene substrate conditions affect the structural arrangement of the epitaxial material, researchers can deliberately manipulate and control the structural properties of the epitaxial material to achieve a range of unique and desirable properties and performance capabilities.

We introduce an innovative approach to determine the number of shared random trends among multiple time series, both in equilibrium and out of equilibrium conditions. This procedure utilizes a test statistic that accounts for the influence of long-term persistence and is robust to the presence of extreme data deviations. Under the assumption of normal data distribution, the estimator's convergence and asymptotic distribution properties can be accurately determined. However, when dealing with non-normal data distributions, the speed at which the estimator converges can be slow and is predominantly determined by the behavior of the central tendency calculation, specifically the sample mean, which is known to be slow converging in the presence of long-term persistence and extreme data. As a result, the accuracy and reliability of the asymptotic distribution are significantly impacted, resulting in a vast bias margin that persists as the sample size increases. Consequently, this phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the analysis of non-stationary time series. A solution to these challenges is offered by the application of a heteroscedasticity and long memory model on the squared differences between the time series observations and their respective trend components. This research is centered on the premise that the dominant behavior of the estimator is dictated by a singular equation that governs the average of the estimated degrees of freedom for the beta-distributed ratio of two chi-squared statistics, one of which is normalized by its sample size, and both of which are calculated at the individual data point level. This framework is extensively explored through theoretical and numerical investigations, with a particular emphasis

By incorporating realistic mass distributions for the host cluster and its surroundings, our research delves into the impact of small-mass objects on the large-scale lensing pattern of galaxy clusters. Our methods involve leveraging the open-source lensing software, pyLenses, which allows for the accurate simulation and visualization of lensing effects. In our analysis, we examine the impact of objects with masses less than $10^{10}$ Solar masses that are embedded within the primary cluster and surrounding shear peaks. Our approach utilizes a combination of source and counter-source reconstruction techniques to quantify the influence of these objects, resulting in a significant increase in lensing delay and distortion on a cluster-by-cluster basis. However, when considering the overall population of these objects, their combined effect is relatively minimal. To better understand our findings, we created in-depth, interactive 3D visualizations of the cluster environment, which can be utilized through our pyLenses scripts also in a standalone mode.

This research explores a scenario in which multiple Internet Service Providers (ISPs) collaborate, leading to content providers experiencing increased rewards and ISPs making more efficient investments. We examine their decisions using a Markov Greedy Process (MGP) model and analyze the resulting equilibrium through a computational method. Our study reveals that cooperation among ISPs encourages investment and improves outcomes for content providers, with the benefits, however, typically being diminished as more ISPs join the collaboration. We also discover that an additional content provider can yield greater rewards for ISPs through cooperation, whereas an increase in content providers can result in lower payoffs for ISPs when they do not cooperate. To promote successful outcomes, we also offer strategic suggestions for ISPs to establish trust with one another and potentially reap better rewards.

In a variable-rich environment, where objects and morphisms can change, the relationship between objects and morphisms retains its essence. This insight forms the basis for the concepts of weak naturality and the weak essence of a functor or a morphism.essence. A weakly natural transformation is a flexible equivalence that remains unchanged under the map $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$. This notion is more inclusive than standard notions of naturality and encompasses instances where the map $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ is not necessarily surjective. When a morphism $f$ is such that the map $\mathrm{Hom}(A,f)$ is an isomorphism for all objects $A$, $f$ is considered to have a weak essence. This paper investigates the properties and characteristics of objects and morphisms with weak essences. It demonstrates that the presence of an object with a weak essence as its base object is a defining characteristic of a category that is abductively complete. It also shows that in such categories, the base object can be uniquely determined by properties of abductive completeness and the characteristics of objects with a weak essence. This paper further establishes that the base object of a weakly essentially closed subcategory is always a reflexive subcategory and that it is uniquely determined by its relationship with objects with a weak essence within it. Additionally, this paper determines the characteristics of objects with a weak essence in relation to objects that are closed under a given equivalence relation. It identifies these objects with a

We introduce a polynomial $\beta$-attractor model that fits the cosmological data and outperforms a previous exponential model. Both models originate from modifications of a power-law potential that, in the early stages of evolution, behaves linearly or exponentially. Following this, we investigate how these models compare to a model consisting of a linear plus quartic potential, previously shown to be a limit of the exponential $\beta$-attractor model. When testing these models against cosmological data, a statistical comparison reveals that the polynomial model exhibits a significantly higher fit than the others. Additionally, we find that the cosmic evolution of the polynomial model is characterized by a rapid growth of perturbations in the early stages, subsequently decelerating as they approach a finite attractor value, in contrast to the exponential model, which exhibits continuous acceleration. Furthermore, we determine the potential and spectral tensor index at attractor and show that the polynomial model fits data equally well when considering only late-time data.

We introduce "filling measured bending laminations" as a key concept for our research. A specific set of these, which we call "maximal filling measured bending laminations," plays a crucial role in understanding the topology and geometry of quasi-Fuchsian manifolds near the Fuchsian locus. Contrary to earlier beliefs, we prove that there exist multiple quasi-Fuchsian manifolds with a given maximal filling measured bending lamination. This outcome has significant implications for many theoretical problems involving hyperbolic manifolds and Kleinian groups. For example, it means that there are an infinite number of distinct quasi-Fuchsian manifolds with the same compact boundary. We also establish the existence of non-Caratheodory conformal structures in the quasi-Fuchsian region that are invariant under the action of PSL(2, R).

This study introduces a novel approach, using the empirical characteristic method, to model individual and collective asset price dynamics by analyzing historical market data. The proposed model leverages observations of cross-sectional return patterns to infer underlying risk factors' behavior, unaffected by common asset price movements. The first four cross-sectional return moments serve as key indicators for the corresponding risk factors' distribution shapes and scales. Applying the empirical characteristic method allows for simple estimation of the model. Our analysis of US equity market data from 1928 to 2019 reveals that cross-sectional return patterns exhibit similar fluctuations to those seen in asset returns, yet with distinct distribution shapes at different horizon lengths. Furthermore, the model's risk factors demonstrate noticeable differences in behavior using period-specific and rolling window estimations compared to an equally-weighted portfolio of the S&P 500 Index Fund returns.

Phonocardiogram (PCG) signal analysis is a fundamental tool for cardiac examination. It's crucial to identify cardiac Coherent Active Regions (CARs) with distinct signal characteristics during the heart's contraction and relaxation phases. We propose using the modified Coherent Active Regions via time-environmentemed (CARET) algorithm to accurately determine CARs from the PCG signal in various environments. The existing approach assumes knowledge of relaxation duration and perfect denoising, which isn't always the case in real-world situations. We've developed a new method that utilizes feature vectors of signals and their surrounding context to identify distinct characteristics and cardiac functions despite noise and uncertainty regarding relaxation duration. We tested this approach with existing denoising techniques, like autocorrelation-based removal of incoherent signals and a confidence interval for relaxation duration based on contraction period analysis, to determine cardiac Coherent Active Regions. We evaluated our algorithm with 168 patients' signals from the standard MIMIC-CRD database and a dataset with 1000 patient's signals from the PhysioBank, which included manual labelings for 40 patients. We compared our algorithm with a previously developed method that assumed perfect relaxation duration and denoising and found that it resulted in low F1-scores of 0.65 and 0.57 respectively on the two datasets. We also studied the results of missed and false detections and found that our approach could be improved by using patient-specific information to enhance model generalization and accuracy in

A detailed analysis of the structural aspects of the excited state of the muonic hydrogen is carried out in this study in order to refine the muon-proton form factor calculations. Our research incorporates the volume effects of the internal structures within both particles, as well as the inherent uncertainties tied to the model of the proton's core, into the form factor assessments. Our findings suggest that the current discrepancy between theoretical and experimental predictions for the 2S transition is primarily driven by the differences in core model assumptions, and that a subsequent measurement of the 3S transition will reveal more insight into the tail regions of both the muon and proton structures.

Let $G$ be a finite group that acts on the torus $T^2$ in a way that has only a single type of orbit. We are asking about the cohomology of this torus when it is factored by the different $G$-orbits. This specific cohomology is represented by the ring $H_{\mathrm{ev}}^*(T^2;G)$, which is unique to even degrees. Our research suggests that $G$-twists play a significant role in this cohomology. To support this idea, we provide a comprehensive proof that $G$-twists are key to determining the entire $G$-equivariant cohomology of the torus $T^2$. Similarly, in the case of a cyclic group action, we find that $G$-twists are sufficient to calculate the $G$-equivariant cohomology of the torus $T^2$. Our research also reveals specific $G$-twists that are applicable to the $G$-equivariant cohomology of the torus $T^2$ when $G$ is not cyclic. Our results provide the first computation of the $G$-equivariant cohomology of the torus $T^2$ when $G$ is not cyclic. Additionally, our research shows that $G$-twists are also relevant to the odd degrees of the $G$-equivariant co

To foster a more inclusive environment in our department, we established a Diversity and Inclusion Committee (DIC) to address these concerns. In our first year of existence, we accomplished several key projects that benefited the department as a whole. This write-up details the DIC's creation, goals, and our initial endeavors to achieve these objectives. Our efforts were crucial in enhancing the department's community and will serve as a benchmark for future DIC initiatives.

A crucial integral operator, known as the fractional series operator, plays a significant role in functional analysis. Researchers have been trying to understand the boundedness of this operator between various function spaces. In this article, we investigate the boundedness of the fractional series operator between $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. It is demonstrated that if $\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}<\frac{1}{2}\alpha-\frac{1}{2}$, the fractional series operator $T_{\alpha}$ is not bounded from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ into $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, we prove that $T_{\alpha}$ is bounded from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ into $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$ when $\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{q}\geq\frac{1}{2}\alpha-\frac{1}{2}$.

The theory of the auction has undergone significant transformation in recent years, 
with a growing number of experiments being conducted to complement it. In this study, 
we explore an aspect of auction theory through an experiment. Specifically, we investigate 
how bidders behave in non-credible second-price auctions when the seller has limited control 
over ensuring auction rules are followed. Our research findings reveal that sellers who can 
punish rule-breaking do not necessarily maximize their revenue, and instead, often award 
the contract at a lower price to bidders who engage in strategic behavior. Furthermore, 
our analysis shows that sellers who can enforce auction rules tend to win fewer contracts, 
even though they have the highest valuation. Our study provides a more comprehensive 
understanding of the conditions under which sellers benefit from enforcing auction rules 
being followed, which has significant practical and theoretical implications.

We explore how cosmic momentum affects spatial anisotropies born in the early universe, assuming the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Wilson model for this phase of expansion. Our research indicates that as the universe progresses from its initial state to the present day, isotropy inevitably replaces anisotropy without any conditions being imposed on the initial conditions, such as de Sitter expansion. Our findings also reveal that any de Sitter anisotropies, such as those resulting from cosmic inflation, will be eliminated by a maximum age of the universe, which is calculated to be approximately $10^{10}$ years. This age is determined solely by the model's scale factor and Hubble constant. Furthermore, our analysis shows that for any given age of the universe, its scale factor can be maximized based on the maximum anisotropy it can support. Our study further extends the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Wilson model to include spatial anisotropies that are more extensive than those of the standard Friedmann-Lemaitre model. Additionally, our results confirm that the standard Friedmann-Lemaitre model is a special case of the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Wilson model, where all anisotropies are minimized.

We establish Gr\"obner fan and Gr\"obner variety structures for specific local defining ideals associated with Hessenberg varieties, utilizing a modified approach that accommodates variable degree limitations. By applying this analysis, we compute Gr\"obner varieties for particular Hessenberg pairs, resolve conjectures regarding their complexity and connectivity, and offer a general approach to determining Gr\"obner varieties for arbitrary Hessenberg varieties.

Using generative adversarial networks, researchers have created a novel approach to capturing the intricate patterns of human brushstrokes. By limiting each stroke to be shorter than traditional brushstrokes, they can generate a sequence of connected dots that can be combined to form compelling paintings. Building on this concept, a new model called BrushGAN continues this legacy by producing individual brushstrokes. To differentiate BrushGAN from existing GANs, researchers have developed a brushstroke classification model to evaluate the generated brushstrokes and found that BrushGAN outperforms current methods in creating brushstrokes that mimic those of real artists. Furthermore, by using BrushGAN to train a generator that produces full paintings, they have achieved results that lay the groundwork for a future brushstroke-level painting algorithm.

We discuss potential New Physics explanations for observed flavor anomalies in $K$ and $B$ meson decays, with a focus on results from $b\to s\ell\bar{\ell}$ processes. Given the differences between these decays, their consistency, and the diversity of flavor violations, multiple New Physics scenarios are necessary to account for all experimental findings. We explore the implications of these anomalies on the $K$ physics system, particularly in relation to $BR(K^0_{\mathrm{L}}\to \pi^0\nu\bar{\nu})$.

Question answering, a fundamental task in NLP, is receiving increasing attention for its practical applications in processing human language. Researchers have developed knowledge-based question answering systems that can retrieve answers from structured datasets, but these are limited by the information available in these sources. To enhance the knowledge base and mitigate these limitations, we've designed a large-scale dataset, called QASPER, which contains over 550K annotated questions. This dataset covers a broad range of topics and was created through a collaboration between Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform and NLP experts, incorporating rigorous validation processes. The dataset's development has far-reaching implications for improving NLP models and enhancing human-computer interaction. In this paper, we'll present the dataset's structure, showcase the results of experiments conducted with it, and highlight its potential impact on the NLP community.

The dynamics of a core-collapse supernova are driven by a complex interplay between the expansion of the supernova and the recollapsing jacket of matter. This process can give rise to the instability known as fast instability, particularly if the supernova explosion is unsuccessful. Recent studies have explored the effects of various physical processes on instability development, but a full understanding of the impact of supernova explosions on instability is lacking. To address this knowledge gap, a series of 3D numerical simulations of supernova explosions were conducted, focusing on the dynamics of jacket matter and supranova core collisions. These simulations investigated how supernova explosions influence fast instability development in jacket matter and its evolution over time. This work includes a comprehensive analysis of fast instability development in jacket matter across a range of supernova explosions and noncollapsing jacket matter cases. Additionally, the relationship between core collapse and fast instability in jacket matter was investigated, including the effects of jacket matter density and radius on instability development. This study marks the first time the effects of supernova explosions on fast instability in jacket matter have been comprehensively examined.

Automated ADHD diagnosis using deep neural networks has gained significant interest in recent years. The primary requirement for deep learning-based models is a vast, well-organized dataset, which our study aims to contribute to by creating. Our data consists of 1054 fMRI scans paired with corresponding clinical data from 369 ADHD patients and 387 non-ADHD individuals. To minimize computational costs associated with data labeling in the training process, our model focuses solely on reducing the impact of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) on the cingulate cortex region. Built upon M-MCTS, our innovative model combines M-MCTS with MTCO efficiently and modifies it into M-TCO-MCTS by integrating MTCO with MCTS through M-CO. Then, M-TCO-MCTS is further refined to M-TCO-MCTS-MO by using the Monte-Carlo method. Finally, M-TCO-MCTS-MO is modified to M-TCO-MCTS-MO-MO by making the omission policy mandatory. Experiments demonstrated that our proposed model, M-TCO-MCTS-MO-MO, yielded superior outcomes compared to other relevant data-driven methods. Specifically, our approach achieved high levels of accuracy, sensitivity, and F1-score of 70.46%, 70.69%, and 70.41% respectively, when trained on just 20% of the relevant regions of interest.

We present a straightforward method for verifying the uniqueness of interior fixed points for a pair of non-linear operators acting on Banach spaces and having a compact interaction region. This framework is versatile and can be applied to a range of operator pairs, including ones that are not identical, as long as their action on functionals is comparable within a specific context. Our results are then used to prove the existence and uniqueness of interior fixed points for models of stochastic games, both individual and competitive, under both classical and extensional conditions.

Acronyms are an essential part of everyday language, with many being widely recognized 
(NAFTA, NASA) while others are less commonly recognized (#FBI) or specialized (#NASA). 
While large language models have made significant progress in filling in acronym knowledge gaps, 
they often fail to account for the context in which they are used. 
This research aims to improve upon previous efforts by leveraging systems to identify potential acronyms 
and associate them with their corresponding expansions, ultimately enhancing the accuracy of language models. 
Through an analysis of 18 distinct domains across English Wikipedia, this model has shown superior performance 
compared to several established models, including 4NLP, Transformers by Hugging Face, and Wikipedia's own parsing system. 
This support for acronyms has been integrated into the Hugging Face model hub, with its code and dataset also available on GitHub.

To address the question of heat transport in quantum Hall systems, we develop a theoretical framework that incorporates heat rectification. Our approach assumes coherent counterflow of electrical and thermal currents, formulation of heat transport equivalent to electrical conduction in the same geometry, and identification of a heat current operator analogous to the electrical current operator. Our method is versatile and can be applied to various quantum Hall geometries, and we demonstrate its efficacy by calculating heat rectification and thermal conductivity in a quantum Hall edge state and a quantum Hall interferometer. Additionally, we show that heat rectification is solely caused by electron-electron collisions through the consideration of a quantum Hall correlator. Moreover, we observe that heat rectification and thermal conductivity are minimal due to the absence of a Wigner fermion fluid, and we discuss the experimental feasibility of observing these phenomena.

A central challenge in DNA data storage is optimizing storage space and access speed.
Our solution involves dividing a large DNA pool into smaller, independent sections with varying capacities, allowing simultaneous writing of diverse files.
By strategically placing specific primer pairs on target sequences, we can control how much data each section holds and where new data is added, ultimately improving both read and write operations.
To achieve better overall performance, our algorithm distributes files across these sections based on their sizes, too.
Our method enhances both the efficiency of DNA data storage and the longevity of stored information, extending the life of each partition by at least six times, or until it reaches half its full capacity.

Topological phases in systems with a continuous spectrum have garnered considerable attention, yet the understanding of topological characteristics in systems with a momentum-dependent band structure remains limited. In our study, we examine a class of systems described by a frequency-independent Hamiltonian with continuous momentum dependence. Through a comprehensive analysis, we establish necessary conditions for zero-energy modes in these systems and derive topological characteristics associated with nodal lines in momentum space. Unlike other topological states, nodal lines in systems with a quadratic band structure can be studied within a two-dimensional framework, with the effective Hamiltonian reduced to a quadratic form in momentum. Our theoretical framework is applied to various systems, including graphene trilayers and hyperbolic graphene, where we identify and stabilize nodal lines through lattice symmetry. Our findings open doors for the experimental investigation and realization of nodal lines using graphene materials.

A study examines how fast information propagates through an array of oscillators connected in a grid structure, giving each oscillator a set of neighbors a unique pulse-producing ability. The analysis focuses on observing wave patterns and measuring their speeds for various oscillator configurations. The results demonstrate that wave propagation in such arrays is influenced by several factors, including the arrangement of active pulse-generating sites, the response of inactive sites to active neighbors, and the pulse-generating site activation duration. To simplify the analysis, the authors developed a model that incorporates only these influential factors, enabling a more in-depth study of the resulting wave patterns and their speeds. The findings indicate that arrays with pulse-generating sites on every grid point produce the fastest information propagation and that certain pulse-generating patterns achieve a limit of optimal speed regardless of the size of the array. The research also shows that different pulse activation periods can either limit the size of the array where optimal speed is achieved or allow optimal speed to be achieved regardless of the array's size. Furthermore, combining these findings with previous studies on active Boolean matrices reveals a broad conclusion that any configuration of pulse-generating sites on a grid can achieve optimal speed for large enough arrays, even if the arrangement looks complex and slow.

To develop reliable entropy estimation tools, it is crucial to create algorithms that work effectively for a wide range of inputs, with their entropy not nearing zero. In contrast to existing methods, which typically require knowledge of the input distribution, this study presents two unsupervised algorithms that can determine the entropy of an information source with a known upper limit on its input entropy. These two algorithms, based on different principles, demonstrate superior performance when compared to established benchmarks, even in the presence of noisy data. By offering these solutions, this work expands the possibilities for applications in fields such as communication theory and coding.

The future of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare is bright, especially with the potential for image-based biomedical research to improve its foundations and make significant contributions to its practice. However, the success of AI depends on the availability of high-quality research data, which involves a complex set of challenges and requirements, particularly regarding data ownership, user permissions and agreements, quality controls and process standardization, as well as the need for versatile and user-friendly access to imaging data and related information. In response to these complexities, we designed an imaging biobank creation framework that addresses these concerns through a collaborative approach, flexible data storage and retrieval architecture, and tailored data acquisition protocols aligned with AI applications. By taking a comprehensive approach to design and implementation, we have developed a functional imaging biobank that streamlines the process of developing and integrating AI into the medical workflow, as evidenced by our successful collaboration with an AI-powered computer vision system to track cellular changes in fixed tissue sections.

Current commercial models for medical diagnosis rely heavily on data augmentation methods such as data transformation and data mixing to improve their performance. However, the effectiveness of these techniques highly depends on the availability of clinical features which they often lack. As a result, their usefulness is limited to more complex and potentially high-risk diagnoses. To overcome this issue, we introduce an innovative data augmentation approach called text generation that produces highly realistic patient descriptions from raw medical code through the use of a conditional generative model called CMS-GP, built on a variant of the VAES architecture. This new approach can effectively enhance medical diagnosis models even when clinical feature information is absent, making it a versatile solution. Our work also highlights the significance of pre-training the conditional model on a large, unannotated corpus, as well as the benefits of incorporating a reconstruction loss in the model's optimization objective function. Our results demonstrate that the application of our data augmentation approach results in a notable improvement of the AUC score for models without access to clinical features, from 0.8401 to 0.8641. Additionally, we experimentally confirm that the generated clinical features possess the characteristics of actual clinical features, including their correlation with the model's predictions and their presence in positive samples.

Polymatroidal ideals, a type of toric ideal, have a unique property - their fibers over non-projective points are smooth. Researchers have developed an algebraic model, the polymatroidal cone model, which utilizes polymatroidal ideals to represent a broad range of toric morphisms. This paper investigates various aspects of polymatroidal cones, including the restriction of linear series, the structure of their fibers, and the composition of polymatroidal cones. These findings are further applied to the study of toric bundles and minimal free resolutions of polymatroidal ideals.

We introduce a quantum version of the K-means clustering algorithm by leveraging superseding operations on q-registers. Our approach results in an asymptotic complexity of $O(\log N + k)$ time and $O(\log N)$ qubits, where $N$ is the number of data points and $k$ is the number of clusters. When $k$ is relatively small, this quantum technique offers an advantageous substitution for classical K-means, enhancing the scalability of clustering tasks. Furthermore, we outline potential applications and challenges associated with its execution using current quantum technology.

The Transiting Exoplanet Survey of Systematic Errors (TESES) project involves re-analyzing data from the K2 campaign to identify patterns in planetary mass ratios. By focusing on smaller mass ratios (up to 0.1), the study builds on previous research by Brasseur et al. (2019), incorporating new and corrected data points, including two newly discovered planetary events. The updated analysis maintains consistency with prior findings, revealing an uneven planet mass-ratio distribution and supporting earlier hypotheses about the existence of a 'desert' around a mass ratio of 0.01, as well as potential evidence for two distinct planet populations with mass ratios below 0.01 and above 0.035. Future work with TESES will incorporate analysis of larger mass ratios (up to 1), potentially providing crucial insights into the 'great desert' between $10^{-3}$ and $10^{1}$ in the planet mass-ratio space.

Shadows can greatly enrich the three-dimensional atmosphere of a scene, 
but determining them through actual ray tracing can be excessively time-
consuming. In our solution, the problem of identifying shadows is partitioned
into two separate sets of triangles: those that cast shadows and those within 
shadows. By isolating and independently processing the triangles within 
shadows, our algorithm significantly speeds up computation. Additionally, by
using occlusion maps to represent which triangles are affected by shadows, 
shadows can be computed much more rapidly. This new approach allows for 
real-time computation of shadows.
The formula for calculating the effect of a light source on a triangle 
$A_0...A_3 $ is given by:
$ \frac{2(V_0w_0+V_1w_1+V_2w_2)}{(A_0w_0+A_1w_1+A_2w_2))} $ 
where $ V_i $ represents the dot product of the light vector and edge $ i $'s 
vector on triangle $ A_0...A_3 $.

In probabilistic O-D demand modeling, data from a panel of households is used in conjunction with observed travel times, to estimate the probabilities of individual households' O-D demands. However, due to the presence of noisy data, accurate demand estimation becomes a challenging task. A new study breaks down this complex problem into two components - the determination of the structure of the covariance matrix and the estimation of the probability distribution of O-D demands conditional on the covariance matrix structure. The study proposes a novel covariance matrix model enhanced by lasso regularization, which yields more robust results compared to the traditional expectation maximization algorithm. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that increasing the size of the data panel can mitigate the impact of sparse correlated errors. The study's findings also indicate that incorporating lasso regularization in a k-means clustering framework can effectively discover the underlying clusters in the covariance matrix and thereby improve the structure of O-D demands.

We have discovered that weak nonlinear frequency dispersion can create conditions which render the stability of phase-locked states in oscillators vulnerable. This phenomenon has been successfully demonstrated in a system consisting of two polarization modes in a fibre, which lock into equal-period states despite weak nonlinear effects influencing their frequencies. Furthermore, we have developed a mathematical approach, based on a phase equation with a small parameter affecting the equation's linearity, and used it to obtain key findings regarding the system's stationary states and their linear stability.

Researchers have created two efficient methods for producing uniform spanning trees randomly, and our study integrates these approaches into a single hybrid algorithm that generates these trees significantly faster than the individual methods. The new hybrid surpasses the efficiency of the currently best-known algorithms by improving the worst-case time complexity or outperforming it in specific situations where a particular generator is used. We also examine the potential for combining the methods with other unique tree generators called p-symmetry and (p+1)-symmetry generators.

Developing comprehensive music datasets is crucial for advancements in music representation learning and cross-modal retrieval. Current music datasets, while useful, are limited in their ability to support learning of rich, semantic music features. To address this limitation, we introduce the MusicTM-Dataset, a comprehensive collection of 1 million music tracks with accompanying lyrics. This dataset enables researchers to investigate the relationships between music and lyrics, thereby enhancing cross-modal retrieval capabilities. To demonstrate the potential benefits of our dataset, we also present a benchmark challenge focusing on music-lyrics retrieval, along with state-of-the-art baseline models and evaluation criteria. The MusicTM-Dataset, as well as associated benchmark and code, are accessible through the repository https://github.com/SMU-DRL/MusicTM-Dataset.

This project's primary goal is to incorporate interactive data visualizations on wikidata.org using Ontodia, a open-source knowledge graph visualizer. By embedding interactive visualizations onto the page, user experience during data explorations can be greatly enhanced. To achieve this, a new feature was introduced allowing users to click on cells in data tables, triggering a visual representation of the selected data as a knowledge graph. This interactive visualisation can be found on the data page for countries and regions. Future plans include expanding this feature to support all data tables and developing a mechanism to automatically detect and highlight data sets for queries and searches.

The theoretical model we investigate involves the coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equation in a two-dimensional setting with semi-infinite space, focusing on dark solitons characterized by a single dark soliton and zero dark solitons as asymptotic background. This model enables us to compute soliton solutions with arbitrary wave speed in the longitudinal direction, whose orbital stability we analyze using the variation method and nonlinear stability method, ultimately establishing the existence of stable solitons for a broad range of wave speeds. Furthermore, we find that solutions initially resembling a moving dark soliton, whose speed converges to a black soliton, exist for all initial conditions, including those containing a bright soliton. These solutions are stable, as proven through the variation-nonvariation nonlinear stability method, thus providing a means to seek orbital stability in the coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equation with the absence of a dark soliton background. Based on this model's results, we can deduce that similar properties likely apply to the bright-soliton solution of the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

The Lotse library serves as a comprehensive resource for implementing guidance strategies across diverse simulation platforms. To enhance its functionality, a new adapter was developed to integrate Lotse with the IDL2000 simulator, which is utilized in the navigation training system of the Dutch Navy. In order to demonstrate the adapter's capabilities, a novel guidance strategy was created that adjusts pilot input to simulate instructor interference during training. This adapter successfully incorporated the guidance strategy, which was subsequently tested in real-time within the navigation training system, yielding favorable results.

The study focuses on optimizing nested flux surface formations within a stellarator design. Stellarators with optimal coil positioning can exhibit highly flexible magnetic scenarios. Advanced optimization techniques are utilized to adjust stellarator design specifications and control coil positions, especially in the outer layers, to precisely manipulate flux surface volumes. Research shows that these optimizations can lead to more versatile magnetic scenarios, extending the range of available combinations for diverse applications. We present examples of optimal stellarator designs, including a design based on the NCSX project and a recent example from recent RAX designs, demonstrating the potential for significant improvements in flux surface volumes through optimization.

A nuclear reactor's utilization of proton resonance frequency (PRF) as an indicator for temperature measurement depends on accurate calibration, especially considering the effects of surrounding materials. The thermal neutron activation of materials within the reactor causes additional neutron capture reactions, resulting in increased fast neutron populations. The influence of these additional neutrons on PRF needs to be taken into account for precise temperature measurement. The research utilizes a refined model of the reactor's zero power critical experiment facility, incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect and incorporating the PRF effect

We studied the behavior of an $N$-species mixture on a fully connected network of $L$ nodes where the local mean-field approximation holds, obtaining an equation describing how $M$ rare condensates emerge and interact. Our research showed that in this system, there are as many distinct condensates as there are species, each forming independently from the others. However, when species interact multiplicatively, there are only $N$ distinct condensates. Our analysis of this model, extended to infinite network size, revealed a phase diagram and the distribution of $M$, the number of condensates, for various ratios of weakly interacting species. Our results were verified by comparing them to a simulation of the model where individual nodes were randomly populated with species. Our results suggest that, on average, there are approximately $\sqrt{N/L}$ condensates in this system. Our results were further extended by studying the impact of adding 'dilute' species, which interacted with other species in a unique way. Our research showed that these species could prevent the formation of large condensates and result in a complete failure of the local mean-field approximation when their interaction with other species changes from multiplicative to additive. Our results were verified by obtaining an equation describing the critical threshold at which this failure occurs. Our research provides a theoretical framework for studying the behavior of complex systems, such as mixtures of light algal species in a tidal marine environment.

We analyzed 26 magnetic phenomena triggered by solar flares moving across sunspots and observed the speed of these sources to vary significantly. Some of these sources moved rapidly at over 500 km/s, while others moved more slowly at around 100 km/s. Interestingly, the sources associated with the strongest solar flares in our sample moved the fastest, on average. Furthermore, the speed of these sources increased in proportion to the logarithm of the solar flare's strength. The magnetic sources we studied in this analysis moved more quickly than previously reported averages for other types of solar phoenomena, and we believe the fastest of these sources may have been driven by shock waves.

We introduce an alternative interpretation of the Madsen-Weiss theorem by applying Taylor's cocycle techniques, which can be categorized under the umbrella of the b-principle. By interpreting the Madsen-Weiss theorem through the lens of the b-principle, it is possible to derive multiple classical stability results in genus 2 and 3 that were initially demonstrated using distinct approaches. Although the connection between the Madsen-Weiss theorem and the b-principle seems non-obvious at first glance, it is actually facilitated by a complex interplay between two key conceptual contributions to the theorem: the introduction of the moduli space of quadratic differentials and the establishment of its Teichm\"uller space as a targeted target space for the Weiss-Manin mapping, combined with the specific nature of the tail of the Teichm\"uller space.

An in-depth examination of the analysis behind a domain decomposition preconditioner known as Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) is presented. The study focuses its stimuli on the basis functions used for coarse grid resolution and the treatment of the preconditioner's local problems. By examining how these components affect the preconditioner's performance, the analysis determines the optimal choice of basis functions and stabilization parameters (lambda) that maximize the convergence rate of the preconditioned Krylov-space solver. The results of this study are verified through experiments with a 2D idealized problem. The outcome identifies the specific basis functions and lambda values that are most effective, adding to the existing body of knowledge that suggests these components are largely independent.

Users play a significant role in categorizing content through tagging systems, with the added benefit of leaving behind valuable research data. This study examines the user tagging process from a psychological perspective, uncovering patterns in how users create tags. Our analysis of over 120,000 tags placed by 367 researchers across five research domains reveals consistent tagging habits within each domain. However, these users do not exhibit the same level of consistency across different domains. These findings suggest that automatic content categorization could be implemented within each research domain but not universally across all research areas. Additionally, our research identifies two potential issues with current tagging systems: the time pressure under which users operate and the lack of guidance provided by existing systems. These shortcomings present opportunities for the design of more effective content management systems that take into account the underlying psychology of human computation.

A theoretical model for low-frequency acoustic waves in single-walled carbon nanotubes has been developed, which takes into account the effects of temperature and molecular interactions influenced by surface modifications. By applying the semi-classical model of quantum mechanics and assuming quick thermalization across the nanotube, the study utilizes a non-equilibrium statistical approach to derive energy and momentum transfer rules at the nanotube boundaries. Through the application of the non-equilibrium Boltzmann-Hubbard model, the transport properties of the nanotinos are determined and further analyzed to design and create new micro-scale acoustic metamaterials.

This study establishes a key result for the FENE dumbbell model, demonstrating that it meets the low-frequency condition. Consequently, it leverages this outcome to derive significant log-H\"older estimates in Besov spaces for the velocity and pressure fields associated with the model. Notably, these estimates are globally valid, covering all time intervals, and are independent of the initial conditions. Moreover, we prove that the model's solutions exhibit logarithmic temporal self-similarity in Besov spaces, which is similar to the behavior found in the Kenzie-Slowikowski model. Our analysis shows that the model's solutions are contained in the space $L^qL^{\frac{q}{2}}(0,T)$ with $\frac{1}{q} < \frac{1}{2} < \frac{1}{p}$ and $p \in (1,\infty)$. As a result, we obtain the estimate $\log(1+t)^{\frac{1}{p}}\lVert (1+t)^{\frac{1}{q}}\lVert f\rVert_{L^{\infty}H^{\frac{1}{p}}} (0,T)\rvert \leq C(t+T)^{\frac{1}{p}}$ for any $q \in (0,2)$ and $p \in (1,\infty)$.

Recent advancements in wireless technologies, particularly in the precepts of shared non-line-of-sight (NLOS) and line-of-sight (LOS) connections, have paved the way for efficient integrated access and backhaul systems. Mobile integrated access and backhaul (mIAB) has emerged as a promising technique to supply high-speed mobile connectivity, making it an essential component of next-generation wireless networks. Leveraging techniques such as user clustering and shared uplink transmission has increased the potential to provide cost-effective and efficient mIAB solutions. Building on this, this article delves into the state of research surrounding mIAB capabilities and future developments, focusing specifically on the key principles and technologies behind user grouping in mIAB systems. Additionally, an innovative approach using a novel hybrid technique to maximize throughput in mIAB systems is presented. This method combines the strengths of existing shared uplink and individual backhaul connections to achieve optimal performance.

When evaluating the stability of algorithm performance, researchers consider the sensitivity of the outcome to changes in hyperparameters. Despite common assumptions, this study reveals that hyperparameters interact with each other in a more complex manner, influencing each other's ranges and impact on performance stability. These findings are uncovered through a novel representation of the hyperparameter space as a Markov process, which allows for the exploration of its geometric properties and properties of the algorithm's error surface. This unique approach has been successfully applied to the task of learning to convert images of hand written digits, using the MNIST dataset and the MNIST-LF extension with local texture information, while being evaluated on the official testing data.

This article examines the quantization of electromagnetic field energy using the Balmer series. We demonstrate how a straightforward mathematical approach can be used to develop the Bohr model of a hydrogen atom, yielding the exact frequencies of the Balmer series. Furthermore, this methodology may be extended to more complex atoms, but the spectra of these atoms will not consist of simple, discrete patterns. We also discuss how our method differs from the initial postulates of Bohr and highlight its similarities to later theories, including the quantum mechanics of Schrödinger and the matter-wave interpretation of de Broglie.

Traditional reinforcement learning environment evaluations often remain static, but in real-world scenarios, problems and conditions evolve over time. An essential aspect of an algorithm's capabilities is its adaptability to varying environments, conditions, and challenges. To test an algorithm's comprehensive performance, we believe it's crucial to assess its ability to adjust to different situations and challenges. Therefore, we introduce a set of RLEs that not only change over time but also ensure a smooth and predictable progression from one state to another. Additionally, we utilize these dynamic environments to investigate a relatively unexplored area of research - reinforcement learning curriculum design. By gradually introducing new elements, such as goals, in a controlled and systematic manner, we show that even basic algorithms can achieve high marks in these ever-changing environments. What's more, our findings indicate that an algorithm's performance is significantly enhanced when the curriculum is carefully tailored to build upon previous achievements, rather than simply presenting unexpected obstacles. To facilitate the widespread use of these advanced RLEs, we provide them as part of the SteadyLearn package, a Python tool that includes the environments, a framework for dynamically generating curricula, and a set of pre-built curricula and pathways.

The multi-messenger astronomical telescope Liger is a 3-meter telescope at the Keck Observatory in Hawaii that operates in both optical and near-infrared wavelengths. Liger's data processing pipeline relies on its Data Reduction System (DRS) which is composed of multiple segments, including a real-time processing engine, various data analysis algorithms, and a user interface. To facilitate testing and development, a test driver called TD underpins Liger's DRS by providing tools for assessing performance and identifying errors. Using a feature-test structure, TD supports both individual and comprehensive testing of Liger's DRS components. Furthermore, with the capability to run tests both interactively and in batch modes against mock and actual data, TD allows scientists to verify the end-to-end functionality of Liger's DRS across various scenarios. By promoting consistency and reducing inconsistencies in Liger's DRS testing, TD ensures uniformity in testing processes, thereby streamlining the testing process and aiding decision-making operations.

The primary objective of this research is to demonstrate the occurrence of a specific type of traveling wave near the Couette flow within a specific viscoelastic system. The analysis relies heavily on a highly nonlinear system derived from the Couette flow, where the occurrence of a singular point is evidence of a nontrivial traveling wave. Consequently, a relevant approximation is made to a highly nonlinear system, resulting in a normal form form with a semi-simple saddle-center equilibrium point. Subsequently, a study of the perturbed form reveals a distinct level of regularity, thereby facilitating an application of the Kruzhkov entropy method to a related partial differential equation system. The resulting solution, although formally expressed, is nonetheless shown to be locally bounded by a specific measure with respect to time and space. Ultimately, a reduction technique is applied to derive an ordinary differential equation, thereby confirming the existence of a nontrivial traveling wave. The given data for this research includes the occurrence of a regular level up to a order of at least 5, thereby fitting the necessary criteria for this study.

Achieving control over polarization is crucial in various applications including spintronics and nonlinear optics. Traditional methods controlling polarization have relied on spin manipulation or using specialized crystals to break symmetry. In this research, a new approach to polarization control is presented, which utilizes a layer stack with embedded thin layers with inherent broken symmetry. By placing a thin silicon dioxide layer between gadolinium gallium garnet and silicon, polarization selection was demonstrated with high efficiency, showing 90 percent polarization at a 45-degree angle, with minimal residual components. This innovation offers a new technique for manufacturing polarization controllers, with promising implications for integration in existing semiconductor processes.

This study investigates a family of nonlinear partial differential equations that incorporate second-order spatial differential operators with a non-local evolutionary term governed by the parameter $\lambda$ in dimensions $d \geq 1$. We explore how the parameter $\lambda$ influences the presence or absence of solutions to these equations, which belong to the critical exponent $2^{**} = \frac{2}{1-d}\left( d + \frac{2}{|m-1|} \right)$ in various function spaces. Moreover, the investigation of solutions to these equations also considers factors such as the sign of $m-1$, the dimension of the domain $d$, and the sign of the measure $\mu$ under partial integrations with respect to $y \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Based on the specific value of the parameter $\lambda$, either solitary wave solutions that are invariant under the transformation $(x, y, t) \to (x, y+te^{\lambda t}, t)$ are shown to be found, or no solutions exist. These results imply that the solutions to these equations exhibit a sudden change from existence to non-existence as the parameter $\lambda$ changes within the set $\mathbb{R}$. Furthermore, the study also provides alternative proofs of the existence and non-existence of solutions to the equation defined by the Kuramoto model for $m = 3$ and $\mu = |x|^p e^{2\alpha |y

South Africa is one of the countries most affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, with a significant increase in deaths and infections according to public health data. However, there are several constraints associated with using publicly available data in South Africa, including incomplete information, incomplete knowledge, data discontinuity and unavailability. To address these challenges and supplement the existing gap in research on temporal spatial modeling of the pandemic, a novel method called the ZTD is proposed. Based on the logistic SEIR, the ZTD combines statistical and mathematical techniques to create an unbiased temporary spatial model. By utilizing time-series and geographical data in reverse, the ZTD uncovers hidden patterns and relationships within observed data, effectively forecasting trends and making precise predictions about future outcomes, including probable infections, deaths, and recovery rates. Notably, the ZTD has demonstrated remarkable predictive power for observating past collisions, including the second wave of infections in South Africa, as well as forecasting future outcomes that align with current real-time data.

We establish that any infinite sequence of integers that are disjoint in pairs and uniformly distributed across arithmetic progressions of a specific spacing can be represented as an infinite sum of subsets with limited terms, expressing these subsets as sums of consecutive terms facilitates our proof that these subsets include any finite arithmetic progression, this conclusion also applies if we allow a limited number of terms in the sum. This finding addresses a question initially posed by Bergelson and Shapiro, along with a related problem proposed by Ko and Bessner; our result encompasses and expands upon previous work by Bergelson and Strauss, yielding a new class of discrete uniform distributions.

This study introduces an approach called hierarchical fusion, a distinct method of combining information from multiple sources in contrast to early, intermediate, and late fusion techniques. We test the effectiveness of this strategy on two tasks: 1) estimating the height of vehicles from radar profiles, and 2) categorizing radar signatures of objects based on their functional attributes. The implementation utilizes deep neural network architectures, specifically the deep multi-task neural network (DMNN) and the fourier neural operator (FNO), respectively. The performance of the hierarchical fusion method is assessed in terms of its ability to achieve comparable results with less training data, a more streamlined training process, and better generalization capabilities. The findings indicate that hierarchical fusion surpasses all alternative fusion techniques examined.

To free up hospital bed space for COVID-19 patients, it is essential to accurately predict intensive care unit admission and treatment duration. We have developed a model that utilizes the September 2020 convolutional neural network architecture, transferred from image data analysis, to evaluate the relevance of medical images in predicting intensive care unit admission and treatment duration for COVID-19 patients. Our proposed system achieves remarkable results, with a 0.8835 AUC value for predicting intensive care unit admission and a mean absolute error of 7.497 days for predicting intensive care unit duration, all through automated hospital chart evaluation. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that model performance can be enhanced by concentrating on critical images and features that are most relevant to prediction, thereby streamlining critical hospital data analysis.

We consider the transmission eigenvalue problem in $ \mathbb{R}^N $ (N greater than or equal to three) for the vector-valued Helmholtz decomposition of a constant vector potential field $ \mathbf{A} $ in a ball $ B_1 $ with medium parameters $ \hat{\eta} $ and $ \beta $ that may vary. We establish that when $ \hat{\eta} $ and $ \beta $ are constant, and $ \mathbf{A} $ is a smooth vector field, the transmission eigenfunctions localize near the boundary of the ball, as the eigenvalue parameter $ \mu $ approaches its essential support. This localization is similar to the one observed in the flat space setting described by Monroch and Zaltsgendler in 2021. Our proof method relies heavily on the analysis of the singular value decomposition of an associated integral operator, which is used to investigate the localization of these eigenfunctions.

Currently, several large-scale pre-training models have been developed for representation learning in spoken language, with certain strategies being used to incorporate additional capabilities. Nevertheless, the effect of multi-task pre-training methods on the representation learning of utterances in spoken language remains poorly understood, with no formal comparison of their capabilities to date. In this study, we compare the capabilities of various pre-training methods, comprising both single-task and multi-task approaches, to establish a comprehensive baseline for spoken language representation learning. Our investigation involves a large-scale corpus of English spoken language, jointly compiled with a massive dataset of written language, allowing for the in-depth analysis of utterance representations. Our findings indicate that multi-task pre-training methods can enhance the representation learning of utterances in spoken language, with our most effective model outperforming existing models in downstream tasks.

The universal fibration over a simplicial group G is constructed as a functor from the category of simplicial groups to the category of simplicial sets, where G acts as a monad.  By applying the monadic embedding, this fibration corresponds to the free group functor from the category of simplicial groups to the category of groupoids.  As a result, the universal fibration can be equivalently defined using the Lawvere theory generated by a group operation and an inverse operation, but with the essential algebraic structure preserved from the group structure in target categories.  Where the universal bundle functor V: SG -> SG's target category SGrp consists of simplicial groups with a free component, a corresponding subfunctor S: SG -> SGrp exists whose target category SGrp' consists of simplicial groups with a free component in SGrp; thus, V is equivalently defined as the left exact left adjoint to the monadic embedding T: SGrp' -> SGrp op.  Where SG consists of simplicial groups with a free component in SGrp, a corresponding subfunctor U: SG -> SGrp exists whose target category SGrp' consists of simplicial groups with a freer component in SGrp; thus, V is equivalently defined as the left exact left adjoint to the monadic embedding T: SGrp' -> SGrp op.
