We present a universal dependency parsing approach tailored to complex languages like Hebrew, which we apply to achieve state-of-the-art results on the new Hebrew UD treebank. This approach is based on a novel, two-stage training method for word embedding and dependency parsing models. The word embedding training is enhanced by utilizing a rich, tokenized Hebrew corpus derived from the Bibles and Sefarim datasets. Additionally, we introduce a new, enhanced sequence-to-sequence model for dependency parsing that surpasses previous conventions, yielding notable improvements. Moreover, we introduce a new, automatic data augmentation technique grounded in the syntax of a language, which significantly boosts model performance. The outcome of our method yields a new state-of-the-art result on the Hebrew UD test set with an UAS of 87.87 and LAS of 86.58. All our code and data have been made publicly available at https://github.com/alecgil/Hebrew_UD_Parsing.

For many years, researchers have been searching for a way to dimension-reduce ell_p spaces in a linear manner. It has recently been proven that such a method cannot exist for any value of p other than 2. However, previous research did find that for odd p > 2, there is a linear dimension-reduction method using matrix transformations. We expand on this by showing that for any odd p > 2, this reduction method can be generalized to non-linear transformations based on the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP). This represents the first non-linear version of the RIP for dimension-reduction applied to ell_p spaces.

To develop a thorough comprehension of a material's history-dependent behavior in solid mechanics, it is crucial to integrate both experimental and computational approaches. The procedure for modeling this behavior typically involves combining experimental tests with numerical implementations of the associated constitutive equations, often following a trial-and-error approach that relies heavily on expert knowledge. We propose a new approach that leverages techniques from continual learning in machine learning to modify existing material models based on experimental findings. The development of our novel learning method is illustrated through a case study that modifies a linearly elastic model to match the behavior of a material that undergoes nonlinear, history-dependent responses.

Researchers examined the performance of various randomly constructed LDPC code ensembles, equipped with an efficient message-passing decoding approach that accounts for noisy channel conditions and random node failures. By combining experimental results with a novel analytical framework, they obtained precise estimates of the maximum permissible error rates for these codes. This analysis also uncovered the significant influence of a code's architectural properties on its overall reliability, demonstrating that some irregular LDPC code constructions can withstand higher error rates than certain regular LDPC code constructions, even those with larger gap sizes. Additionally, it was found that LDPC code ensembles exhibiting negative degree-degree correlations can tolerate higher error rates than those with positive correlations, suggesting a link between degree-degree correlations and code reliability. Furthermore, it was observed that the maximum permissible error probabilities for LDPC code ensembles are generally higher when the distribution of node degrees follows a Poisson distribution than when it follows a Gaussian distribution.

This paper introduces the SL-MPSF method, an incremental predictive control approach that guarantees safety for linear systems under certain conditions and bounded disturbances. By leveraging Lagrange multiplier adjustment and a modified Multiple-Sharpening Filter, SL-MPSF generates safe and optimal trajectories, differing from the standard MPSF method in its ability to account for time costs and bounded disturbance constraints. Unlike MPSF, SL-MPSF is susceptible to termination due to disturbances and may generate suboptimal trajectories when no safe trajectory exists, although this suboptimality is limited by a pre-defined safety margin. By incrementally adjusting Lagrange multipliers and utilizing first-order optimization, SL-MPSF achieves a high level of efficiency, making it suitable for real-time control applications. Various systems, including a robotic arm and a quadcopter, demonstrate the efficacy and performance of the proposed method.

A proposed quantum key distribution system uses decoy states in pairs with weak and strong levels, paired with vacuum state, and sends them through a lossy medium where an opportunistic eavesdropper can affect the states without being detected. By only interfering with the weak-vacuum decoy state pair, the eavesdropper can create a success criterion that overstates the presence of hacking, effectively making the system appear more secure than it actually is. This method can be improved by only interfering with the weak state, which allows the system to appear even more secure. Our study also finds that the proposed system can reach similar levels of security and randomness as a full decoy state system with significantly reduced cost and enhanced resistance to side channel attacks that target the metropolis basis.

Recent advances in large language models have demonstrated a connection between language modeling performance and the ability to undertake specific tasks through in-context few-shot learning. However, the relationship between language modeling metrics such as perplexity and the ability to accomplish in-context few-shot tasks is not well understood. To investigate this, we developed and tested a high-throughput in-context few-shot learning platform that incorporates a diverse set of tasks with comprehensive human benchmarks. The results from our study indicate that there's no guarantee of a correlation between low language modeling perplexity and performance in in-context few-shot tasks. In fact, the relationship between language modeling quality and few-shot task performance is highly dependent on the specific task at hand. Additionally, we found that weight tying, a technique that adjusts language modeling to align with the specific task format, can significantly boost few-shot learning performance.

Even after a decade since the initial discovery, the issue of how cooling catenary matter in galaxy clusters grows remains a topic of debate. Various factors have been proposed as contributing factors, including but not limited to convection, turbulence, and magnetic fields. This paper explores an alternative explanation by taking into account the role of anisotropic heat transfer in the equation for cold gas growth. By reexamining the assumptions underlying previous studies, we found that anisotropic heat transfer results in a greater rate of cold gas growth compared to the established value. Specifically, if conduction is restricted to a particular direction, it can occur more quickly than if it were uniform in all directions. This finding could be particularly relevant to the recently observed bright cold fronts within galaxy clusters. While our research provides a more accurate mathematical model, it does not resolve the debate on the role of anisotropic heat transfer in cooling catenary matter growth. Further observations and simulations are needed to fully understand this phenomenon.

A measurement of $C\!P$ violation in the $C\!P$-odd fragmentation function of $\Xi_c^-$ baryons is made possible by a sample of $\Xi_c^-$ baryons produced in proton-proton collisions. With a data set collected by the LHCb detector at proton-proton collisions corresponding to $9.1\newcommand{\fb}{\mathrm{~fb}^{-1}}\fb$ of integrated luminosity, the $\Xi_c^-$ baryons are detected in the kinematic region of proper lifetime $c\tau\sim 300\mu\mathrm{m}$, proper transverse momentum $2< p_T < 15\mathrm{GeV}/c$, and rapidity $2.5 < y < 4.5$. The $C\!P$-violating asymmetry in the $C\!P$-odd fragmentation function is found to be consistent with zero, offering restrictions at a $95\%$ confidence level. This discovery provides the initial observation of $C\!P$ violation in a beauty baryon and reveals distinct differences from theoretical models predicting $C\!P$ conservation. Additionally, this study provides further evidence of $C\!P$ violation in charm systems, reinforcing the theory that a non-conservation of $C\!P$ exists in the standard model with quarks containing charm.

We've derived a set of new high-energy scattering amplitudes for strings, which confirm and build upon a previous conjecture about string theory's high-energy symmetry. These new amplitudes, calculated using a particular ratio of vertex operators, align with a recent approach to string theory's Regge behavior. We've also found that our derived amplitudes are consistent with the intrinsic symmetry of the string itself, which is a more fundamental aspect of the theory than any specific model. These new amplitudes, calculated to second order, serve as a benchmark for testing string theory's predictions in the high-energy regime.

A key factor in the effectiveness of edge computing is optimal resource management. To achieve this, a multi-dimensional model of energy-vs-performance was created, allowing for the calculation of energy consumption and task processing times. Based on this model, a co-design framework for hardware and software was developed to find the optimal balance between energy consumption and processing times. This framework was solved using two optimization strategies: initial solution optimization and fast convergence optimization. The results showed a 50% reduction in energy consumption and a 30% reduction in processing times when compared to a random allocation strategy. The consequences of these optimizations were then analyzed, including the variations in edge node performance and the resulting effects on users and the system. The long-term consequences of these optimizations were then analyzed through a game-theoretical study, which found that users would benefit from better performance and system stability.

Natural speech encompasses a diverse range of sounds, including repetitive, rhythmic patterns and dynamic, sustained phonemes. Current text-to-speech systems are based on statistical models that generate speech by combining a limited set of basic sound units, often ignoring the inherent transitions between them. In an attempt to produce more natural speech contours, researchers in speech synthesis strive to create models that can effectively capture and replicate these transient sound shifts. A new approach, outlined in this report, is to use a dynamic theme discovery method that identifies and categorizes speech segments across various levels of detail. An innovative continuous theme discovery algorithm is developed to organize speech data by assigning weights to basic sound units and evaluating how well they fit into each category. A continuous version of the Clauset-Neiman dynamic cluster algorithm is also used to identify repeating patterns in phoneme-level speech data. In this study, we focus on creating a continuous speech model for a specific dialect of a specific language using weight-sharing and a varying number of basic sound units. The resulting models are then used to produce a continuous speech spectrum by replicating the weight assignments across different time intervals. An evaluation of the synthesized speech, replicated with weights from a corpus of spoken phrases, suggests that the use of continuous themes results in a more dynamic and sustained reproduction of the original acoustic characteristics.

To optimize motion planning for multi-limbed robots, we introduce a multi-stage optimization strategy, effectively decoupling a complex hybrid system into manageable stages. Each stage is defined by a constrained dynamical system, whose optimization is solved in advance using parallel computing to expedite motion planning. We employ Model Predictive Control to adjust parameters in real-time, ensuring that a trajectory meeting pre-set connectivity and timing requirements is generated. These trajectory segments are secured over a predetermined look-ahead horizon, allowing adaptive adjustment within this period. We illustrate the performance of our proposed method using a simple quadruped model.

In our research, we establish a method to effectively convert highly valuable quantum states into their corresponding lesser versions with reduced errors using the distillation technique. This new approach allows us to identify the optimal trade-offs between the levels of these valuable resources and the errors made during the distillation process. We validate the efficacy of this distillation method by applying it to two specific contexts: one based on quantum entanglement and another based on quantum coherence. Furthermore, we derive a mathematical formula that estimates how efficiently this distillation process uses the valuable resources. We also observe that when there is no constraint on the errors made during the distillation, this formula calculates the optimal trade-off values. These results provide us with a greater understanding of how to effectively convert valuable quantum states into their lesser versions with reduced errors.

To investigate how a cup of coffee moves when pushed across a flat surface, researchers from the University of Leicester conducted an in-depth study. They tested the possibilities by moving the cup with the handle as the pivot point, as this is a common scenario in real-life situations. To collect data, the researchers used slow-motion videos of the cup in motion and applied a sophisticated method called the MatLab algorithm to track the center of mass accurately. This information allowed them to examine the subtle movements that occur when the cup oscillates and use theoretical frameworks to analyze these motions in detail. By comparing their experimental findings to established predictions from the research literature, the team evaluated how different factors influence the cup's behavior. By adjusting parameters such as friction levels or the force applied, the study provided comprehensive data on how these variables impact the cup's movement and made significant contributions to understanding complex non-linear dynamics through practical applications.

This paper develops a communication-efficient method for large-scale, distributed learning models by modifying the Decentralized SGD with drift (DR-DSGD) algorithm. We analyze the mean squared error (MSE) convergence of this updated approach, which closely resembles stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in terms of iteration efficiency but exceeds it in communication requirements. The tightness of our MSE convergence estimate is also assured. Compared to other communication-efficient DR-DSGD variants, our method offers a significantly improved convergence rate, particularly as the number of devices grows. We validate the theoretical performance through experiments using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets in a distributed setting with multiple devices.

The concept of entropy production has been integrated into the modeling of nucleus-nucleus collisions in order to improve our comprehension of entropy generation in the early stages of these events. Pre-equilibrium entropy production is calculated using a thermodynamic model based on the equation of state and initial energy and momentum distributions. By incorporating this model into the AMPT model, which features multiple-scattering processes, a direct relationship between initial conditions and final collision outcomes has been established. Specifically, the relationship between pre-equilibrium entropy production and the number of charged particles in the mid-rapidity zone has been investigated via simulated data. Our results demonstrate a positive correlation between these two factors, which suggests that higher entropy production during the early stages of collision leads to increased yields of charged particles in central nucleus-nucleus interactions.

The initial stage of protostar formation, including the collapse of a core and the formation of a protostar, is not well understood due to the lack of mass and energy exchange processes in core collapse. In order to study this process, we simulated core collapse and protostar formation by modeling the core as a gravitationally bound, rotating, neutral gas and employing the enzyme model to convert kinetic energy into thermal energy, as well as the EBS equation of state for low-density plasma. In our simulations, we found that the core collapse leads to the protostar's early envelope mass losing a significant amount of mass and energy via a thermal flare-accelerated mass loss and radiative thermal expansion, with the protostar's radius expanding to hundreds of astronomical units and its luminosity increasing to thousands of times that of the solar nucleus due to the energy released from the protostar's early envelope. However, if the protostar's early envelope does not experience a thermal expansion, its collapse leads to a thermal expansion and radiative thermal expansion due to the energy released from the protostar's early envelope, with its radius expanding to tens of astronomical units and its luminosity increasing to tens of times that of the solar nucleus. In our simulations, we found that the protostar's early envelope experiences a thermal expansion if its mass is less than about 0.95 times the core's mass and its kinetic energy is more than about 6.8 times

From a mathematical modeling perspective, a method is proposed to address a limitation in current linear complementary formulations that cannot capture complex relationships between destabilizing effects and system safety. A complementary formulation is developed that incorporates destabilizing effects variable (DEVA) directions, enabling the identification of safety-critical areas and the calculation of minimum safety margins with respect to DEVA directions. A convex optimization algorithm is developed to determine the optimal DEVA directions that ensure system stability and minimize safety margins, thereby resolving the original NLP optimization problem in the DEVA space. Numerical tests demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing approaches and can efficiently determine optimal DEVA directions for balancing destabilizing effects and system safety.

The Sun's radiation pressure, reflecting the Sun's brightness as seen from the object, significantly impacts its orbital movements in the solar system. This pressure can place objects in resonant orbits that cause their shapes to change. An numerical analysis was conducted to examine the effects of this pressure on objects in a specific orbital category. Results indicate the occurrence of varying rotations and changes in orbit. An approach to reduce the uncertainty associated with these predictions is developed. This involves representing the uncertainty in a specific astronomical value related to the object's orbit and utilizing Monte Carlo simulations to forecast the resulting uncertainties. Applying this method to a group of asteroids yields the following outcomes: the uncertainty in predicting the changes in their orbital shapes is negligible compared to the uncertainty in predicting their spin changes; the uncertainty in predicting the changes in their orbital eccentricities is somewhat significant; the likelihood of observing objects with highly inclined orbits experience significant changes in their rotational period. This theoretical analysis may be applied to objects with direct solar radiation as the primary external force influencing their orbits.

In the context of tight-binding models, the standard approach uses a spatial basis to describe the states of atoms in a material. However, this "velocity gauge" approach has limitations, especially when dealing with non-local interactions and long-range effects in insulators and superconductors. An alternative "vector potential" approach can rectify this issue by incorporating curl operators into the basis. Yet, this reformulation often introduces anomalies into the descriptions of electromagnetic responses. We present a novel method to eliminate these anomalies by introducing a non-local correction based on a controlled approximation of the band structure. This procedure works by approximating the hydrodynamic tensor of the electronic fluid and then projecting the vector potential basis to match the approximate tensor. We have successfully applied this method to two-dimensional dirac semimetals, accurately extracting the correct velocity and susceptibility within the approximated regime. Furthermore, our method can also correct for misaligned band touchings and accounts for a quantum kinetic term describing non-local exchange processes. Our approach not only improves the accuracy of electromagnetic responses but also provides a direct connection to the physical properties governing these responses.

In many computer vision tasks such as pose and shape estimation, keypoint correspondences are often relied upon but found to be error-prone due to factors like scale and translation discrepancies, making outcome vulnerable to noise. The traditional robust regression techniques, although effective in certain scenarios with minimal outliers, are often surpassed by graph-based methods that utilize geometric principles to perform robust fitting. The proposed method leverages a graph-theoretic approach to achieve resilient shape and pose estimation in the presence of noise by representing keypoint correspondences as a conflict-minimization problem on a graph. By employing a geometric framework to resolve this conflict and performing resolution through graph optimization, the proposed method yields superior outcomes with minimal outliers. We demonstrate its efficiency and robustness using complex real-world datasets such as ModelNet and KITTI, leading to substantial improvements over state-of-the-art techniques and even closer alignment with ground truth when only a small number of outliers is present. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashish2109/ConflictMin.

The paper centers around the development of a confidence region for the parameters of a Cauchy distribution, based on a sample of complex data. A confidence region is established, expressed in terms of the sample quantities $\bar{z}$ and $S$, with the caveat that this construction is inherently linked to the behaviour of a random walk in the complex plane. Additionally, the paper highlights the distinctions between this approach and more traditional methods for generating confidence regions, focusing on the challenges posed by the inherent 'noise' in the estimates for the Cauchy distribution parameters.

In clinical trials involving subgroups without shared treatments, typically observed at specific intervals, subgroups tend to reflect similar characteristics. Our analysis shows that borrowing information between these subgroups can significantly lower the required trial sample size. To facilitate this process, we've created a predictive model using data from previous trials to estimate treatment effects in new, unknown subgroups based on similarities with existing subgroups. This approach enables us to conduct a trial comparison using data from multiple subgroups simultaneously, allowing us to identify potential subgroups with promising results and prioritize resources for subgroups where there's already strong evidence. By doing so, we enhance trial efficiency in discovery phases without sacrificing validity. Our method is applied in two case studies, one involving Alzheimer's disease and another with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, both resulting in improved statistical power for identifying treatment effects. Our analysis indicates that borrowing information between subgroups can be a valuable tool in discovery phases, helping researchers to make more effective use of available data and resources.

Effective placement tracking is essential in various motion control systems, and tracking performance can be significantly influenced by dynamic conditions. The usual assumption of constant velocity or acceleration may not be sufficiently dynamic to support high-performance placement tracking. To address this limitation, we propose a tracking method that utilizes state-dependent dynamics and provides an exact solution for optimal tracking performance. Specifically, we have successfully tested our approach in a context of robotic arm control, employing a function that models robotic movement as a mass-spring-damper. The results of our simulations have demonstrated the tracking performance can be substantially improved when dynamic conditions are taken into account.

We introduce a technique that enables the adaptation of pre-trained point cloud registration networks for object classification tasks. The method involves transforming the registration network's learned point to object correspondences into a suitable classification representation. Experimental evaluation on the ModelNet40 dataset reveals that our technique successfully bridges the gap between registration and classification, resulting in improved performance with the same base network when compared to networks trained from scratch. Additionally, we demonstrate that our technique achieves consistent results across various point cloud registration architectures, highlighting its versatility. The main advantages of our approach are its ease of implementation, a lack of additional computational requirements, and the ability to achieve classification-level performance without the need for object-centric scenes. The code for our method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mimilom/pcr2cls.

For a finite group $G$, the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree is the least value of $n$ for which every homomorphism from a free abelian group of rank $n$ to $G$ is trivial. In 1963, Finkelstein discovered the upper limit of this value of $R_\infty$ for any group $G$ is $d_G+1$, where $d_G$ is the maximum degree of imprimitivity of $G$. We derive an expression for $d_G$ in terms of the commutator degree $d_{[G,G]}$ and the length of the core of the commutator subgroup in $G$. Additionally, we establish an expression for $d_{[G,G]}$ in terms of the degrees of imprimitivity of the commutator subgroup of $G$.

A next-generation linear collider, such as a proposed e+e- or muon collider, will be an essential tool for precisely determining the top quark mass. A potential new approach involves using pairs of associated production of the top quark and boson to make this measurement, but this production will typically occur at a low energy below the W boson threshold. In this research, we develop a realistic simulation and associated analysis of a hypothetical top quark measurement at a muon collider with a demonstrator or low-energy upgrade, focusing on the challenging scenario of insufficient data due to limited luminosity or a smaller collider. We examine pair-produced top quarks without W bosons and explore reconstruction methods utilizing the four-lepton decay of the Higgs boson when it is produced in association with a top quark. In this particular scenario, with an integrated luminosity of 10 ab^-1, a top quark mass resolution of around 0.9 GeV is achievable. Although this research centers on a muon collider, its concepts and ideas can also be applied to a high-energy e+e- collider or future hadron colliders that will utilize precision top quark measurements.

In ultrafast experiments, extracting key information from dynamic spectra demands an accurate reconstruction technique beyond conventional approaches like phase-based methods and neural networks. The new method presents an inversion approach that utilizes model knowledge and integrates data from multiple sources, addressing common issues like data noise and limited spectral resolution. The method excels in situations where phase information is incomplete or uncertain, and it outperforms existing methods in simulated data from a chemical bond's dissociation and a molecule's excited state. The proposed algorithm also utilizes constrained spectral phase retrieval's advancements, and it's compatible with spectral and temporal constraint information. The technique's capability to expand to additional constraints makes it highly adaptable to complex problems in ultrafast spectroscopy.

Using lattice QCD with a heavy quark and two light quarks at 2.38 GeV, a study has examined the distribution amplitudes of the $\psi$, $\psi^(*)$, and $D_s^(*)$ mesons. A key comparison was made between the light and heavy quark distribution amplitudes to identify any differences. Results indicate that the $\psi$ and $D_s$ mesons exhibit similar distribution amplitudes yet, surprisingly, the $\psi^*$ and $D_s^*$ mesons exhibit distinct distribution amplitudes. Moreover, the heavy quark in the $\psi$ and $D_s$ mesons is predominantly at the center with minimal momentum distribution, whereas the heavy $s$ quark in the $\psi^*$ and $D_s^*$ mesons is more evenly distributed. This difference is hypothesized to influence the transition matrix elements involving these mesons and their resonances.

This paper offers a straightforward proof that the growth of a function is limited by the growth of its Fourier transform within a specific space of smooth functions, and the estimate's inverse is also proven. In addition, the paper provides estimates for the growth of a function in terms of the growth of a distribution's kernel within another class of smooth functions.

Recent research has put a strong emphasis on developing effective instance segmentation methods combining convolutional neural networks and fully convolutional networks using the SiSi and SiSGAN approaches. However, these methods are prone to producing incorrect class assignments due to the reliance on non-differentable operations such as max-pooling. To mitigate this issue, our proposed CySGAN method circumvents class alignment problems by replacing max-pooling with cyber pooling, a differentiable operation that maintains feature connectivity. The CySGAN framework consists of a cyber network, responsible for capturing instance features, linked with the SiSGAN's differentiable approach for class prediction. In our experiments, the proposed method, consisting of CySGAN-FCN, MTCYNTO, and MTCYTO, outperformed current state-of-the-art instance segmentation methods on the COCO dataset, with a notable performance boost of 3.3% in terms of the mean intersection of unions.

In computer vision, action anticipation has become a crucial element for various applications, especially in gesture-based interaction. A key challenge in gesture recognition is distinguishing between similar gestures, such as handing versus giving a handshake. Existing methods depend on video data from RGB cameras and achieve success rates of 70% with the state-of-the-art CNN architecture, but fail to account for the relationship between different joints in the human body. By incorporating the spatial relationships between different body parts, we propose a new architecture that leverages the capabilities of both 2D and 3D CNNs in a way that allows the model to focus on disparate maps simultaneously. Additionally, we introduce a novel kernel, the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel, to model the connections between various body parts and anticipate actions more accurately. Our comprehensive experiments were conducted on the Charades action dataset, which is considered the gold standard in the field. Before presenting the new architecture, we addressed potential issues with data labelling on the Charades dataset by implementing a new protocol to split the data into training and testing sets. Our experimental results demonstrate that the new model, which incorporates an RBF kernel and multiple convolutional layers, outperforms previous approaches by achieving a 78.6% accurate rate for action anticipation, which represents a significant improvement of 10% compared to the previous best result of 68.6% reported in the literature.

The Hubble Space Telescope's STIS instrument observed a solar-like star, AT Microbe, during a stellar flare event. The 1999 observation included both the hydrogen line at 6680 angstroms and a far-ultraviolet continuum from 1350 to 1650 angstroms. Since then, this star has been monitored regularly by the TESS space telescope, allowing for comparison to other flares' spectral patterns. By analyzing these comparisons, it was found that broadening of the hydrogen line is closely linked to the star's optical and far-ultraviolet continuum properties during flares. Additionally, a far-ultraviolet spectrum was obtained from a different telescope, showing fluctuations in the 1350-1650 angstroms continuum. These two observations are discussed in the context of flare emissions rooted in accelerated particles, and the findings are then compared to other flares' spectral patterns, including those from larger, cooler stars.

We initially establish that abelian G2-instantons exhibit rigidity, meaning they remain unchanged under isospin transformations. Additionally, we derive an algebraic condition for G2-instantons to be non-abelian. Furthermore, we show that the non-abelian G2-instantons with a specific topological invariant have a particular charge of -4.

This study investigates the $C$-normality of two types of operators, $P_{\varphi}$ and $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are analytic functions on a specific domain in $\mathbb{C}^2$. It examines how the properties of these operators rely on the functions $\varphi$ and $\psi$, as well as the operator $C$. Furthermore, the paper provides essential conditions for $C$-normality in terms of $\varphi$ and $\psi$.

We establish a key relationship between the $p$-cores of $p'$-partitions and modular arithmetic. This connection enables us to determine the number of largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions for a given prime $p$, by effectively counting the number of solutions to a particular modular arithmetic problem. By leveraging this counting process, we derive a formula for the largest $p$-core partitions of $p'$-type. Furthermore, our research leads to the creation of a rapid-convergence series representing the generating functions associated with $p$-core $p'$-partitions.

Recent research from Wang and Zhang demonstrated that Point Cloud Networks (PCNs) can be reinterpreted using different dimensional spaces for point representation, leading to new insights into PCN generalization. This new understanding enabled the creation of a precise framework, called the TPC framework, which certifies PCN generalization across various dimensional space conditions. However, Wang and Zhang's findings only considered linear point representation and thus left unanswered the question of whether their framework applies broadly to all dimensional spaces for point representation. To address this question, we demonstrate that PCNs relying on transformations like rotation, flipping, and stretching do not impact point dimensionality. Nonetheless, we also show that PCNs depending on transformations like shearing, shifting, or combining these operations are not able to benefit from the TPC framework's certified accuracy assurance. In response, we propose a new approach - the MTC framework - which not only provides a certified guarantee for more complex transformation cases but also achieves higher accuracy assurance compared to the original TPC framework. Ultimately, our certified accurate errors significantly decrease while maintaining generalization performance as evidenced by our experiments using the PointNet model and the ModelNet dataset.

We're investigating the operation of Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar in crowded environments with multiple transmitters and no central control, resulting in chaotic and disjointed data sequences with unknown start and end times within defined range gates. To analyze radar performance without synchronous timing, we develop a rigorous mathematical model for individual FMCW radar signals and the signal pattern generated when multiple radars operate simultaneously, enabling us to derive a formula for the probability of radar interference within a given time and range interval. This formula enables us to calculate the probability of disjointness for two radar signals within a given time and range interval and apply it to estimate the average data transfer rate, or throughput, in bits per second, for a network of radars within a crowded environment, assuming each radar segment has a defined length and signal strength. Through numerical examples, we demonstrate that our model's throughput estimates match the theoretical maximum throughput in bits per second in the radar network.

We've observed a significant entangled two-photon absorption event in a nonlinear material by utilizing a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram's visibility. The phenomenon occurred when we utilized a continuous wave laser at 1550 nm to generate coherent two-photon states through a process involving spontaneous four-wave mixing in a highly nonlinear optical fiber. Subsequent detection of the interferogram's visibility revealed an entanglement proof of approximately 70%, corresponding to a two-photon correlation coefficient of 0.75. Notably, our findings demonstrate that visible detection of the Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram can serve as an efficient method for identifying entangled two-photon absorption in nonlinear materials, thereby facilitating further applications in quantum information systems.

We establish that $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology on an elliptic curve $E$ is isomorphic to the ring of $T$-equivariant modular forms on $E$. This result is an outcome of combining two theories: that of elliptic cohomology and of weight-one modular forms. Though $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology places $T$ as a coefficient, it does not introduce $T$ as a factor. The isomorphism we establish therefore supports the analogy that draws a paralllel between $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology and $T$-equivariant weight-one modular forms as $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology and $T$-equivariant weight-one modular forms both feature the action of $T$, have a ring or braided structure, and both feature the ellipse $E$ as a key component.

This research introduces a innovative approach to temporal knowledge graph completion, where we suggest a cycle-aware time-encoding method that considers the circular nature of time by taking into account the relative time differences between events. Unlike existing methods that only focus on the linear time frame, this scheme also incorporates more precise time information from knowledge graphs. We develop a cycle-based time embedding scheme and demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing the performance of existing models on datasets MSquared and QuAD, where our results reveal that models employing this new approach achieve higher scores compared to models using linear time encoding.

The distinctive sound of footsteps is often absent in impact sound simulations, except in cases of soft surfaces and heavy falls. To address this, a new substructure for simulating audible ground sound has been developed, applicable to a broad range of scenarios. It comprises two primary components: a weight-drop substructure for surface deformation, and a radiation substructure for sound propagation. This model has been successfully implemented in a CFD code, demonstrating its effectiveness in simulating audible ground sound for a variety of scenarios, such as a person jumping, a falling block, and a landing parachute. Simulation results have shown excellent agreement with experimental data. This substructure is now freely available as a open-source update to the Navier-Stokes-CGF solver.

Quantum systems can exhibit Bell nonlocality, a phenomenon where random outcomes from two distant experiments are interconnected. However, achieving this withinefficient correlations, where there's some underlying order in the data, poses a challenge. In fact, research indicates that it's impossible to perfectly eliminate all remnants of order left behind, a concept known as the zero-order Bell nonlocality. But what happens when the constraints are relaxed just a tad? A new study reveals that it's possible to create non-perfect but significant correlations, weakening previous assumptions that order must necessarily decline into complete randomness. This discovery could be applied to the development of error-resilient quantum information technologies, where a certain level of order may be tolerated. In addition, the findings suggest an expanded understanding of order, which is quantified using a metric called hypergraph, in the context of Bell nonlocality. To put these results into perspective, the study includes concrete examples of systems comprising up to four and eight parties.

The presence of flat bands in molecular structures, characterized by full orbital degeneracy, holds significant potential for achieving flat band superconductivity and other novel electronic phenomena. Intentionally introducing random fluctuations into these systems through chemical disorder can lead to a significant increase in the degeneracy of flat bands, thereby expanding their influence. Utilizing the model of a diatomic chain composed of dimerized germanium and tin, this study investigates the effect of random fluctuations of germanium site occupation on the band structure, revealing a substantial increase in the degeneracy of the flat bands under these conditions. A theoretical explanation is provided, along with a comparison to numerical results obtained via exact diagonalization. Additionally, this study explores the system's properties in the presence of external perturbations, such as light, to assess their influence on the expanded degeneracy of the flat bands.

To understand the properties of hydrogen boride (HB) monolayers, we investigated the electronic and atomic structures of HB, considering various core excitations of boron and hydrogen. Our results from ab-initio calculation demonstrate that hydrogen's presence significantly affects the phonon structure and electron behavior in the HB monolayer, compared to the situation in metallic boron nitride. We found that when using a precise density functional, we can reproduce the phonon spectrum from experimental data, provided a specific exchange-correlation model is applied that accounts for van der Waals forces. Our study of HB monolayers reveals unique properties, influenced by the core-excitation of boron, with its lattice structure exhibiting two distinct patterns and a'molecular' picture resembling CH and similar molecules. Additionally, we identified unique features in electron spectra, influenced by the interactions between electrons and phonons, and observed the effects of van der Waals forces on the electron energy bands, different from those in graphene. Our calculation of two possible sub-strate lattice structures shows that the properties of HB monolayers can be adjusted through substrate design. With the potential application of HB as a superconductor, our research on its electronic and atomic structure, influenced by hydrogen's core excitations, enhances our comprehension of its phonon structure and electron behavior.

The formula for $f_{n, k}$ can be derived from the expression for $e_{n, k}$, which counts the flattened partitions with no restrictions on the size, through a recursive relationship. The process of converting an $e$-combinatorial object to a flattened partition involves merging adjacent elements with similar properties. The number of ways to accomplish this is equal to the third left coordinate of the object's weight vector, plus one. Groups that exhibit virtually nilpotent behavior in character space correspond to algebraic KAM theory, where actions are geratically transitive but not necessarily expansive. In contrast, toroidal dynamics represent a distinct form of action that is expansive in character space. We aim to demonstrate that for virtually nilpotent groups, there is an infinite number of invariant subspaces in character space with respect to any non-trivial element of the group, whereas toroidal dynamics are characterized by a lack of such subspaces. Additionally, using the framework of quantum ergodic theory, we establish that for virtually nilpotent groups, the average case behavior of the longest action of any non-trivial element on the space of characters is of the order $\log n$, in contrast to the scenario presented by toroidal dynamics where the order is linear.

The verification of complex driving systems through model checking has become the industry standard in the automotive sector. The use of model checking, integrated with testing, is recognized as the most effective method for validating and ensuring the safety of driving systems. The verification process involves checking a driving system's behavior in various scenario templates using specific safety criteria. When a system's behavior is found to be at odds with a particular safety criterion in a given scenario, this discrepancy is recorded as a counterexample, which can then inform system modifications to rectify the issue. Although driving systems are inherently dynamic, encompassing elements such as location, velocity, and time, current model checking techniques overlook these aspects, resulting in inefficient checks due to the need to manually validate whether a system's current state allows it to progress to a desired future state. This paper proposes a new, integrated formal safety analysis method that not only automates safety verification but also enables the systematic identification of effective countermeasures to improve safety. The proposed approach begins by translating complex driving systems and scenario templates into a predictable pattern of change. This translation allows for the incorporation of time, velocity, and location variables in scenario templates and the definition of permissible system evolutions. Next, a network-based safety verification method is employed to verify driving systems in various scenarios. The extended Koopman operator theory provides an efficient approach to studying complex dynamic systems that cannot be solved analytically. This methodology involves observing a nonlinear system through multiple observables, which are then used to identify the system's dynamics on a data-driven basis. In contrast to traditional Koopman theory, which operates with smooth observables, the extended theory accommodates general, discontinuous ones. This flexibility enables the theory to be applied to a broader range of systems, including those with chaotic characteristics. However, the practical challenges of identifying the system's Koopman operator, especially for higher-dimensional systems, remain significant obstacles to their theoretical capabilities. Despite these limitations, the extended Koopman operator has been successfully utilized in various areas, such as data-driven control design, which has inspired the development of an intuitive control algorithm based on the theory. This approach aims to determine the necessary control actions for observing matrices based on a linear combination, which ultimately facilitates the efficient control of complex dynamic systems.

This paper explores Leibniz's views on infinity, analyzing how various early interpreters understood his concepts of bounded and unbounded infinity, and how these interpretations were often aligned with Leibniz's calculus doctrine. Leibniz's own writings on infinity are diverse, making it necessary to consider his broader scientific and philosophical context. We examine key early interpretations by Bertrand Russell, Erik Åkerwal, and Paul Noguera to highlight the diverse roles attributed to infinity and to explore alternative possibilities. Our discussion centers on whether infinity should be understood as a methodological or metaphysical concept, and whether it should be seen as fundamental to Leibniz's thought or simply a tool for systematic philosophy.

The most comprehensive photometric survey ever conducted, the Legacy Survey Deep Field, has released its final data layers after a three-year observation period across the southern sky. With its unprecedented depth of magnitude 24.6 at a 3 sigma confidence level, this survey features 10,000 square degrees of space, with nearly one-third of the sky covered by 13 broad photometric systems ranging from UV to near-infrared wavelengths. Building upon the foundation laid by previous Legacy Survey Field of View fields, this data layer includes an advanced point source extraction system that utilizes sexually ambiguous point source information to significantly improve accuracy across the entire sky. With an average yield of 39 million sources, the LSDF's astronomical catalog boasts an unprecedented level of sexplicity. Consider a Hilbert space R^N equipped with the Gaussian measure, and a contraction operator T that maps vectors to vectors in the same space. The measure of a sequence of vectors S_n > R^N is defined as the set of all vectors that approach the operator T with respect to the weak topology, where the sequence S_n converges to S. Under the assumption that the sequence S_n is uniformly bounded, it can be proven that the occurrence of a finite measure for the sequence's image S_n implies that the sequence remains linearly independent. Based on this discovery, it can be proven that certain operators which contract the R^N space are capable of generating sequences that approach the operator T with respect to the weak topology, while also maintaining a strong linear component. These results can be extended to a broader class of measures by appealing to Stein's measure dependence theorem. Furthermore, it can be shown that a correlated noise limit theorem can be applied to a class of weakly dependent polynomials known as multilinear polynomials, which are fundamentally distinct from linear polynomials. Finally, this research, which was initially based on a study of adaptive algorithms, now appears to be a unique approach to probabilistic physics-chemistry modeling.

Transferring knowledge from more informative items to less informative ones with sparse data is a critical challenge in enhancing recommender system accuracy. Our innovative framework, K2V, addresses this issue by leveraging document modeling and a knowledge transfer approach. It consists of two primary components: the context-aware knowledge transfer module, which uses a multi-head mechanism to identify target and source item representations, and the context-aware knowledge injection module that transfers knowledge from more informative items to less informative items within the user's document. By doing so, K2V improves the recommendation accuracy for users with sparse data and enhances the performance of state-of-the-art baselines on various benchmarks.

Conjectures linking large deviation principles for matrix integrals have been proposed by Eldan and Shyamala, showcasing significant connections between conditional freeness and the behavior of matrix eigenvalues. By applying these conjectures to triangular models, we've successfully derived large deviation principles for various eigenvalue ensembles, such as the bulk, edge, and real/spectral components of GUE and BEU matrices.

Real-time systems are dependent on timing constraints and need to be monitored to prevent and detect critical failures. However, traditional monitoring strategies do not take into account the uncertainty that can occur due to hardware and software discrepancies, and thus may lead to incorrect decisions. This can cause some errors to remain undetected and perhaps even falsely confirm others. In order to overcome this limitation, this research proposes a monitoring approach called ARMON, which not only recognizes but also explains the occurrence of errors. By incorporating a model of the monitoring system and the monitored application, ARMON can perform two types of analysis - one for calculating the possible range of monitoring delays and the other for determining the timing discrepancies of the monitored software components. This research further offers a method to calculate the maximum number of errors that can be hidden due to the monitoring delays. By utilizing these results, a decision support tool is provided that helps choose the most suitable monitoring strategy to guarantee the detection of critical failures. Lastly, a case study is presented to illustrate the practical implications of ARMON, and to demonstrate that even simple monitoring strategies can effectively detect critical failures despite the occurrence of minor errors.

Our study of the process $D_s^+\to D^+\pi^0\pi^-$ utilizing 25 fb$^{-1}$ data from the BESIII experiment reveals the presence of an expected signal belonging to the $a_0(980)$ resonance. After accounting for background contributions using multivariate techniques, the production rate for the $a_0(980)$ resonance is calculated to be $2.8 \pm 0.8\times10^{-3}$ with a 95% confidence level, where the calculated cross-section is found to be 0.35 pb. Additionally, the experiment observes no evidence for the $f_0(980)$ resonance in the same process, resulting in an upper limit on its production rate at 4.6 pb (the 95% confidence level).

The GRAVITY project at the Very Large Telescope (EUTM) is one of the key projects at the Millilarge Telescope Project (MLTP), aiming to implement a new adaptive optics system. This innovative project aims to improve the resolution of the MLTP by incorporating a new technology. The proposed adaptive optics system will utilize a novel telescope called the adaptive optics system, featuring a 1 meter aperture telescope. The proposed system utilizes a new technology called the Shack-Hartmann sensor, which includes 12 sensors utilizing a unique reference laser system. The reference laser system breaks down into 32 sub-beams by a reticular pattern and provides efficient coverage of the 2.8 arcseconds field of view. The proposed system utilizes a specific algorithm called the pyramid wavefront sensor and the tomographic data reconstruction method called the GRAVITY data reduction method. We examine the approximability of the Capacitated k-Center problem, a crucial subproblem of data clustering. Our analysis reveals that the Capacitated k-Center problem has a more challenging approximation hardness compared to its outlier-ignoring counterpart, the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem, for any fixed k value greater than one. To establish this result, we reformulate the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem as a special instance of the prize collecting traveling salesman problem, then demonstrate that removing certain edges from the resulting tourist route does not alter its total distance in a significant way. Our finding implies a roughly log^2(k) approximability lower bound for the Capacitated k-Center problem. We also explore more general variants of the problem, allowing for fractional solutions and incorporating metrics other than Euclidean distance, but these modifications do not significantly improve approximability. Furthermore, we prove that tight characterizations, obtained through linear and quadratic programming, can be useful in constructing approximate solutions for the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem and its special case, the Capacitated k-Center problem with approximate metrics. To achieve this, we enumerate all tight characterizations based on sublinear programming and derive an efficient algorithm by restricting certain characterizations and applying the Farkas Lemma in a constructive manner. Our study also leads to the development of an algorithm with a sublinear time complexity that can solve the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem, even when given approximate

This study establishes the precise version of the Brück conjecture for entire solutions $f$ of the Monge-Ampere equation on the complex plane, given that the solution has a hyperorder less than $1/2$. The precise version states that if the hyperorder of $f$ is less than $1/2$, and $f$ is not expressible as a polynomial plus a bounded function, then the inclusion $J^+f = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |f(z)| \to \infty\}$ holds. The proof relies on the confirmation of the hybrid estimate for the solutions of the Monge-Ampere equation under certain conditions.

Our findings improve polynomial linear system solving over finite fields by providing methods to solve systems with fewer evaluations than required for error-free cases, using both Gleason modes. Additionally, our techniques confirm the extension of the Berlekamp-Zibibigniew theorem for finite fields and extend it to prime powers, allowing for the identification of unique factors in finite fields.

We suggest an experiment to produce controlled simultaneous photon emissions in sets of two or more photons by utilizing a multi-atoms cavity QED system. The procedure involves applying two distinct optical pulses to a collection of two-level atoms in a cavity, with the pulses differing in phase and arriving at the cavity at specific intervals based on a classical control signal. The atoms are initially prepared in an entangled state through a process called quantum entanglement purification. When the pulses interact with the atoms, they induce the emission of synchronized photons from the cavity, which can take the form of a combination of even or odd groups of photons. To observe the photon emission in sets, a double-slit setup is used, where the light is split into two beams that are then detected by two photometers, enabling the measurement of interference patterns associated with even or odd groups of photons. Alternatively, we suggest an experiment in which a granular distribution of photons is observed by directing the emitted light through a diffraction grating.

Utilizing experimental data on alkali metals, we develop a comprehensive equation of state through a mathematical equation that incorporates the principles of correspondence across different states for sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, and francium. The equation of state is defined by three interdependent variables: volume, pressure, and temperature. It is devised from a polynomial relationship with continuously varying coefficients, ensuring that the principles of correspondence are adhered to. Furthermore, this equation of state is compatible with the widely-used Debye model for describing thermal vibrations in solids. It also passes through points that represent equilibrium conditions at zero temperature, where pressures and temperatures are arbitrarily variable, and satisfies the regularity condition at the classical transition point (normal-to-suppressed phase transition), thus farlessly incorporating it into the classical approximation of the thermodynamic critical behavior model. Consequently, this equation of state predicts a universal temperature parameter, called the critical temperature parameter (in the classical approximation of the thermodynamic critical behavior model), that is identical across all alkali elements.

We've investigated the effect of a Chern-Simons term on vector mesons in a medium where local parity is violated, drawing from the vector-dominance model and effective lagrangian techniques. Our findings show that in this particular context, the Chern-Simons term contributes significantly to vector-meson properties. Additionally, our study included an examination of the lattice- QCD results for vector-meson mixing and a Chern-Simons term, as well as a brief discussion on the implications of our results for electromagnetic vector-meson mixing.

We introduce a randomized distributed algorithm to estimate the overall size of a network in a sparse structure, suitable for degenerate networks. When initiated from a single node, it relies solely on local neighborhood information and produces accurate estimates within a predefined margin for networks of arbitrary degree. Notably, it outperforms existing methods in terms of efficiency, both in terms of time complexity and communication frequency. Furthermore, when initiated from multiple nodes, it can determine the network's size to within a specified error bound. We provide analytical performance guarantees along with a detailed case study that compares our approach to other estimation methods.

A new finite-volume method is introduced to solve the Hamiltonian constraint within the setting of conformal gravity. This approach diverges from conventional methods that typically require estimating conformal factors or developing custom finite difference schemes on a flat metric. Our method, however, allows for a uniform finite-volume discretization of both the conformal factors and the Hamiltonian constraint without exception, regardless of the gravity model's complexity. To address the challenges posed by the singularity of the conformal factors, a variational approach is utilized in conjunction with an average-value principle. To demonstrate its efficacy, our proposed method is implemented in a specific setting involving a gravitational wave's conformal trajectory.

The 20-kt underground JUNO experiment employs large liquid-scintillator detectors, utilizing synchronized photomultiplier tubes to capture low-energy neutron events. This experiment's neutron event detection approach, though precise, has a limitation in depth resolution due to the non-proportionate PMT responses. To overcome this limitation, we developed an algorithm utilizing the time-of-flight of neutron events detected at different depths within the water layer above the detector to provide enhanced depth resolution. This algorithm was tested using actual JUNO data from a 300-ton prototype and demonstrated a significant improvement in depth resolution, from approximately 75cm to as low as 40cm.

The Informer model has shown remarkable performance in long-term monidimensional sequence forecasting but struggles with multidimensional sequences, which are common in forecasting real-world data with multiple feature dimensions. A key challenge lies in our current understanding, which fails to effectively capture inter-dimensional relationships, though they are crucial for precise predictions. To address this limitation, we propose Enhanced Informer for Multidimensional Sequences (EIMS), a modified version of the Informer model. To handle multidimensional sequences, EIMS employs a new adapter module based on an attention mechanism between different feature dimensions. This adapter allows the model to focus on important dimensions and their inter-relationships, which enables it to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant dimensions. To improve long-term dependencies, EIMS increases model parameters in both adapter and encoder modules. Experimental results on widely-used multistep time series forecasting datasets demonstrate EIMS's superiority over existing baselines, including state-of-the-art models like Prophet and LSTNet.

The quality of a telescope's vision can be severely hampered by atmospheric dispersion due to different colors being refracted at varying angles. Despite being a critical element in telescope design, there is a notable lack of research on this topic, particularly concerning the sensitivity of refracted colors to the altitude and variation in the stars' spectral ranges. In our study, we utilized the Rayleight formalism to develop a precise analytical model for atmospheric dispersion that is easy to understand and has a high level of accuracy. By comparing our model to existing models, such as the Hubble and V-band models, we found that it outperforms them in the red spectrum but falls behind in the blue spectrum. However, our model remains superior to the alternative "effective radius" method that is commonly used to design ADCs and produces a more realistic refracted circle that is better suited for applications in the blue spectrum. As a result of these findings, we recommend using our atmospheric dispersion model in conjunction with the V-band model for most telescope operations and considering the effective radius method as a suitable alternative for ADC design in the blue range of the spectra.

Current top-tier ensemble models, like those utilizing pairwise predictions, struggle to exploit label information due to its indirect impact on prediction confidence. To address this, we introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel approach that iteratively utilizes label information to refine predictive logits through a series of backward passes, eventually yielding superior results compared to leading ensemble models within the pairwise prediction framework. PILE's computational efficiency, particularly in the prediction phase, is on par with other contemporary models. To facilitate training with multiple models, we employ a gradient-based optimization method and develop a specialized optimizer, Adaptive Weighted Elastic Fusion, for adjusting learning rates within multiple models. To verify the robustness and generalizability of PILE, we perform thorough experiments across diverse datasets, model architectures, and training settings, ultimately showing its exceptional performance in handling hard labeling, partial labeling, and multi-task learning scenarios.

The current research search for dark matter inspired by the Oxford group's work uses multiple detectors to analyze signals produced by ultra-light bosonic dark matter. By cross-referencing the data from various sensors, we have refined our approach to discarding both random variations and genuine signals. We have additionally examined signals over time, allowing us to better distinguish actual signals from mere noise. Our revised methods are capable of enhancing the threshold for identifying genuine signals by up to fifty times, as well as lengthening the amount of time in which we can effectively observe these signals. The basis pursuit problem, a linear regression with bounded-coefficient error, can be transformed into an optimization task with a matrix and vector. When dealing with sparse solutions, the proposed strategy involves specifying a spectrum - a range of values that represent the relative strength of solutions - and utilizing this in basis pursuit with degree distributions that match certain criteria. By analyzing the condition number of the matrix, which affects basis pursuit's ability to find sparse solutions, this work provides an algorithm to determine an optimal spectrum. The basis pursuit problem with this optimal spectrum yields a more robust sparse solution. Additionally, this method is applied to other problems, such as basis pursuit with bounded coefficients and total variation minimization, and yields improved performance.

Advances in programmable switch technology have led to increased research in switch-aware networking. However, existing research faces a significant challenge due to the lack of accessible, modifiable compiler backends, making it difficult to conduct in-depth driver-level analysis and develop new applications. To address this gap, we have developed an open-source toolchain allowing researchers to create custom packet processors using a high-level language and simulate them on a range of programmable switches. This toolchain provides a novel approach for researchers to implement new ideas in switch architecture without needing direct access to hardware. By using this toolchain, we have implemented multiple innovative concepts, demonstrating its effectiveness and adding value to the field. Furthermore, the source code and documentation for this toolchain are freely available for other researchers to use, modify, and contribute to.

We propose a novel finite element approach that effectively solves the vector transport equation, a fundamental model used to describe fluid flow and scorpion flow in a coral of fire. By utilizing vector transport equations, we can calculate directional dependencies in scorpions, but existing transport equation solutions often have inaccuracies and oscillate due to refined meshes in the direction of the flow. To overcome these issues, we have developed a mixed finite element method that combines the vector transport equation with the standard continuity equation. Consequently, the solution space for the vector transport equation is extended, and it becomes possible to handle a slightly divergent flux field. The outcome is a more stable method that effectively handles vectors and makes implementation easier for users. Our time-transient simulation results demonstrate the second-order accuracy of the proposed approach, and it outperforms existing methods that are only first-order accurate.

To address ethical concerns in AI, the machine learning community has proposed various methods to mitigate biases in training and model inference. Despite these efforts, a significant knowledge gap remains regarding how these methods actually affect fairness in real-world applications. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by investigating fairness in federated learning with differential privacy. We examined how fairness metrics are affected by combining techniques such as constrained optimization, quantization, and statistical filtering. Our experimental study provides insights into the trade-offs between fairness, accuracy, and privacy under different scenarios, which can inform the development of new transparency methods. We hope our findings will encourage the adoption of more transparent and transparent model-building practices.

A detailed analysis of the $B_c^+\rightarrow J/\psi p p$ decay process has been carried out across different momentum ranges of the $J/\psi p$ system. The investigation involved examining the $J/\psi p$ invariant mass spectrum at low energy and also across its entire energy range, both with and without an underlying momentum correction. The result showed that there are two excited $B_c^+$ states, namely the $B_c^{\ast +}$ and $B_c^{\ast +}(2S)$. The $B_c^{\ast +}$ state was found to have a mass of 6823.1 MeV/$c^2$ and was seen to be closely aligned with the $B_c^+$ state, whereas the $B_c^{\ast +}(2S)$ state was found to have a mass of 6871.4 MeV/$c^2$. Both $B_c^+$ states were found to have a decay width of approximately 11 MeV/$c^2$ for a branching fraction of $10^{-4}$ of the $B_c^+ \to J/\psi p$ decay process. The result was found to agree with the predictions made through the relativistic independent quark model.

Our analysis shows that continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods can be seen as solutions to certain Hamiltonian differential-algebraic systems. Additionally, we examine their application to solve certain types of Hamiltonian ODE problems that are inherently nonlinear. By reinterpreting these methods in the context of Lagrangian mechanics, we observe that the resulting numerical solutions do not conserve the Hamiltonian function, although we found that certain conservative numerical methods can be derived from existing Hamiltonian formulations. As an example, we apply and studied two continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods, before concluding by evaluating their effectiveness on various precise problems.

Model training criticism is a valuable tool for optimizing neural network training. The conventional approach criticizes global training practices, which often result in uneven learning among convolutional and recurrent modules within the network. By focusing on local areas, such as individual layers or groups of neurons, more targeted feedback can be provided to the teacher, facilitating more efficient and module-specific training. We evaluate the effectiveness of local critic training across three convolutional and recurrent neural network architectures and find that it significantly improves their overall performance.

In our study, we establish the existence of Wada points in a system that experiences chaotic scattering, which implies the presence of a basin boundary that forms an M-shaped figure. Moreover, we demonstrate that this system possesses a stable Wada basin even under weak dissipation. Our research focuses on a simple model involving a particle moving under the influence of a weak dissipative force in a region near a critical point where two potential functions intersect. This is in contrast to previous studies, which generally required a high level of dissipation to observe Wada basins. Building on this finding, we broaden the theoretical framework and explore a general model of dissipative system, which is defined by a set of nonlinear differential equations with a weak dissipative force. This model facilitates the identification of Wada basin boundaries through numerical analysis, which has been successfully applied to several systems, including a logistic map with a weak dissipative force and modifications to the three-body problem in celestial mechanics that incorporate a weak dissipative force.

To investigate the muon g-2 anomaly, we propose an experiment known as LDMC that will leverage the high-intensity muon beam at the muon accelerator and a magnet with an extremely close proton-proton collision point. This experiment has the potential to be carried out at several facilities, including the Future Circular Collider (FCC-hh) and the Compact muon solenoid-like experiment (CMS-mu). This study focuses on the design of the LDMC experiment, taking place at the FCC-hh where an extremely compact proton-proton collision point with a short decay length is utilized to collect 12.7 ab^-1 of integrated luminosity over a 10-year period, spanning multiple FCC-hh design phases and muon beam energies. This experiment will investigate the muon g-2 in previously explored and unexplored regions, offering novel discoveries and sensitive tests for numerous beyond-the-standard-model theories, including dark sector and axion-like particles, heavy charged scalars, leptoquarks, and supersymmetric models. This study presents separate, independent results for either a muon beam with an energy of 4 GeV or 8 GeV, demonstrating either a 0.5 sigma or 4 sigma detection potential for various theories. For example, assuming the presence of 0.008 ppm dark current that directly interacts with the muon, we project a 4 sigma detection margin by collecting 12.7 ab^-1 of integrated luminosity

Human attention shifts throughout time and space in a complex and subtle way in response to various stimuli. Achieving a similar level of precision and flexibility with machines is a challenging task in video analysis. A potential solution is the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), which seeks to mimic human spatial and temporal attention mechanisms in a more systematic way. By designing HAN with modules that focus on important areas within sub-frames and time periods, researchers aim to improve low-complexity action recognition performance on challenging datasets such as Mini-Kinetics. The HAN approach surpasses existing weakly-supervised recognition methods with higher accuracy, especially at low complexity levels.

As the black hole's energy diminishes, its state transforms into an extremal state characterized by a fixed energy. Consequently, the initially dispersed scalar energy, which took the form of fragmented waves when we first analyzed the extremal scenario, merged into a singular oscillatory pattern in the extremal case. In contrast, the oscillatory fragment waves persisted in the near-extremal case. However, the process of the black hole transitioning from a near-extremal to an extremal state can be slowed down by subjecting it to a scalar field. Moreover, the impact of the black hole's initial state, which either preserves or destroys the scalar field's structural integrity, is also observed. In the near-extremal case, the scrambled scalar energy that survived from the scattering process could be released back into the black hole's quantum state.
